Further, Raje underlined the need to take "urgent steps" to amend the existing constitutional provisions to provide for "at least 10 to 20 per cent reservation in the interim in favour of the Economically Backward Classes".

A week later, on January 23, a senior official from the Tribal Affairs Ministry wrote back to the Rajasthan Chief Secretary stating that the state government had "simply forwarded" the report of the High Powered Committee (the Justice Jasraj Chopra Committee) "in view of the persistent demand of the Gurjjar community for inclusion in the notified list of STs".

"There is no specific recommendation, with justification of the state government of Rajasthan, for inclusion of the Gurjjar community in the Scheduled Tribe list of Rajasthan, either in an area-specific manner or for the entire state of Rajasthan," the Tribal Affairs Ministry wrote.

The ministry further asked the Rajasthan government to examine the report of the Chopra Committee and send "specific recommendations with justifications" if it wanted the Gurjjars' case to be considered by the ministry.

Asked whether mere recommendation from a state government could guarantee inclusion of a community into the ST list — considering that the Rajasthan government's recommendation to include Gadia Lohar and Banjara communities was pending since 1981 — Kyndiah said: "It is not easy to accord ST status. The number of people classified as STs are around eight crore now and the cake is getting smaller. Further, those already in the ST list are opposed to including more communities in that list. We have to be very careful of the repercussions that could arise out of any move to accord ST status to any community."

Heading: ArcelorMittal joins bid to acquire sick steel company in Amethi - Indian Express
Content:
Mulayam Singh Yadav's Samajwadi Party (SP) is all set to roll into a significant position in Kerala's coalition politics from mid-July. And, one of the two men pulling the SP wagon into Kerala will be Abdul Nassar Mahdani, the man who was in jail for nine years as a prime accused in the 1998 Coimbatore serial blasts that killed 58 and maimed over 200, before the court finally let him off for want of enough evidence.

Mahdani chairs the People's Democratic Party (PDP), which he had formed after its earlier and more virulent form, the Islamic Sevak Sangh (ISS), was banned. PDP sources told The Indian Express today that Mahdani will formally merge his outfit by next week with the SP, after he returns from a West Asian tour. A senior Mahdani aide, however, said the PDP had also been weighing the option of "collaborating closely" with the SP without a formal merger.

Mahdani, who has had 32 cases of communal incitement charged against him, has been claiming a very close proximity to Mulayam, both before and after the Coimbatore blasts. He had met Mulayam twice in his office while he was Defence Minister, he had told The Indian Express, and had campaigned for the SP during the UP Assembly elections.

Mahdani's PDP, which had risen to fill the vacuum caused by the eroding base of a steadily weakening Muslim League in Kerala, had changed focus to broadbasing the PDP into a Dalit-Muslim-Backwards platform on an anti-Brahminical and anti-upper caste premise.

But most of the mainstream outfits occupying the Dalit-Backwards space in Kerala refused to ignore his radical islamist tag, and the idea floundered. The PDP, however, has been steadily widening its niche vote bases and getting close to claiming a critical mass in several constituencies.

The other Kerala leader pulling the SP wagon with Mahdani in Kerala will be M P Veerendrakumar, former Central minister and state president of the trouble-torn Janta Dal (Secular), which has decided to merge with the SP next month _ it was really a toss up between the Rashtriya Janata Dal and the SP.

JD (S) sources said Mulayam, who called on CPM general secretary Prakash Karat in New Delhi today, has got the Left's assurance that the JD(S) can remain a part of Kerala's Left Democratic Front even after the merger.

Heading: A murder’s clues: fake NREG rolls and forged signatures - Indian Express
Content:
Global steel czar Lakshmi N Mittal has entered the race for acquiring the Vinay Rai-promoted Malvika Steel, a sick company with its factory in the backyard of Congress general secretary Rahul Gandhi's Lok Sabha constituency, Amethi.

Malvika Steel, which proposed to set up a 6.5 lakh integrated steel steel plant in 1998, never actually got off the ground. It had taken loans to the tune of Rs 1,800 crore from a consortium of banks and financial institutions (FIs) led by IFCI Ltd. IFCI itself, sources said, has lent Rs 600 crore to the company whose plant is spread over 740 acres at Jagdishpur in Amethi.

While about 1,000 workers were laid off in 1998, sources said, there were only about 200 workers who are still hoping the plant would be revived.

The company started defaulting on loans way back in 2001 and was subsequently taken over by FIs, who have moved the Debt Recovery Tribunal to get "whatever they can" by selling the company. The DRT has set a reserve price of Rs 207 crore for the beleaguered steel company.

According to FI sources, the fight for ownership of Malvika Steel has now entered a decisive phase with the DRT likely to receive bids from interested parties over the next two days. Besides ArcelorMittal, the other interested companies are the state-owned steel major SAIL and the Rs 4,000-crore infrastructure conglomerate, Jaypee Group. When contacted, an ArcelorMittal India spokesperson said the company would not comment on rumours.

The company, promoted by the Rai family, turned sick soon after the plant was set up, following which FIs took over the company and approached SAIL and Tata Steel with a takeover proposal. After due diligence, the state-owned steel major agreed to bid for the company but the promoters were unhappy with the price offered by SAIL. Subsequently, Jaypee group offered Rs 207 crore, which was matched by SAIL.

Sources in FIs said the DRT was seized of the matter and hearings were likely to conclude by June 3. The BSE-listed company has been in the red for the past many years and ownership issues have stalled progress in the takeover of the company by prospective suitors.

Malvika Steel had envisaged expansion worth Rs 3,000 crore, but this was left unfinished in 1998, within just 10 months of starting operations. The plant was initially planned to have a capacity of 8 lakh tonne of sponge iron and 1.2 million tonne of iron pellets, but it was converted into a 6.35-lakh-tonne integrated steel plant for manufacture of long products used extensively in the infrastructure and construction business.

Meanwhile, public sector engineering consultants Mecon advised SAIL against acquiring the entire assets of the company. Sources said MECON had found only the iron-making facility of Malvika Steel a viable purchase. SAIL had approached Mecon to evaluate the viability of buying the iron-making facility. After it submitted the report, the lead financial institution, IFCI Ltd put its foot down, saying it was not interested in partial sales, they said.

SAIL then went back to Mecon to evaluate the project as a whole and prepare a feasibility report on the existing assets at Jagdishpur to determine whether there was a need for pumping in additional funds to make it operational as a fully integrated steel plant.

Heading: Unbecoming of servicemen  to protest in public: MoS Defence - Indian Express
Content:
On Monday, the development economist Jean Dreze flagged off the social audit of NREG schemes in Chatarpur, the same block in Palamau where his colleague Lalit Mehta set up Vikas Sahyog Kendra, an NGO, in 2002.

Chatarpur is less than 3 km from Khendra-Khurd village where Lalit had undertaken a social audit of pond project two days before his body was found on May 16. The pond is being dug by the forest department.

"A CD of the social audit was in my son's possession. The CD showed large-scale irregularities. I suspect this led to his murder," said Jagdish Mehta, Lalit's father.

On Monday, during the social audit, more than a dozen persons lodged complaints against officials and contractors implementing the NREG schemes in Chatarpur. "There is too much corruption here. If this is not contained, it will be very difficult for the scheme to take off," said Dreze, one of the prime movers of the UPA's flagship project.

The audit that Dreze's team did in Chatarpur's Rs 5-lakh pond project, after Mehta's murder, revealed several irregularities:

• Muster rolls were not kept at work sites. Job cards were not updated. Payments were not made regularly.

• In the muster, there were 108 names. When the team visited the site on May 17, it found eight workers.

• The signatures of workers were forged. The team established this fact by comparing the signatures its members obtained with samples maintained by the department.

• Urmila Devi, a worker, was illiterate and could not sign. But the muster roll carried her signature in Hindi.

• The signatures of a dozen residents such as Vikram Singh, Ranjit Singh and Santosh Kunwar who had reportedly migrated and not returned were found in the register.

After he was told about the findings by Dreze on May 21, Palamau Deputy Commissioner N.P.Singh ordered an inquiry into the findings.

Heading: Iron lady - Indian Express
Content:
The continued protest by ex-servicemen against the Pay panel's recommendations have started to irk the government with Minister of State for Defence M M Pallam Raju coming on record to say that "it is unbecoming" of former soldiers to take to the streets to press for better salaries.

Sources say the Minister's public rebuttal has a background. The ex-servicemen's sustained dissent has displeased many top officials as armed forces do not have a tradition of going public with their grievances. Sources said that even the PMO has taken exception to this with Prime Minister Manmohan Singh discussing the issue with Defence Minister A K Antony during the last two weeks.

The tipping point, sources said, came after Tuesday's unprecedented hunger strike across the country. "It is unbecoming on the part of dignified ex-servicemen (to launch such protests). I don't think they should be doing this...It is uncalled for," said Pallam Raju, speaking at the sidelines of a CII-sponsored defence seminar in the capital.

The government's argument is that the intensity of the protests is uncalled for as a redressal mechanism has already been put into place and a revised pay structure has not yet been finalized.

Also, the protests continue even after Cabinet Secretary K M Chandrashekhar told Army Chief General Deepak Kapoor last week that the issue is being resolved by the Committee of Secretaries (CoS) and protests and noises of dissent within the armed forces would not help matters. The Army Chief is learnt to have distanced himself from the protests by ex-servicemen.

On May 17, during a presentation by pay cells of all three services to the CoS, some members of the committee took exception to some presentations that "ran down" other uniformed services including the paramilitary and the Indian Police Service.

What further complicated matters was a letter by Navy Chief Admiral Sureesh Mehta to the Defence Minister on the pay panel, written four days after the presentation, that did not strike the right note with the CoS.

The letter raised two points: one, that nothing was being done on the pay review after a meeting with the Defence Minister and, two, there was no representation of the armed forces on the pay review panel.

The CoS took exception to the letter pointing out that the pay cells did make presentations barely four days before the letter.

On the demand of an armed forces representative on the panel, the view is that the pay review is taking place for other services, too, and a "government process" has already been initiated into the matter, of which the Defence Secretary is a member.

Heading: These rivers of life - Indian Express
Content:
• The manner in which Vasundhara Raje is handling the Gurjjar agitation is shameful in a democracy like India. Statesmanship demands not seeing right and wrong but putting an end to the killings. But the CM seems to have descended to the level of the agitators, thus demeaning her office. Whether police firing was necessary or not is something an independent judicial enquiry should settle. Raje hasn't put her best foot forward even in dealing with the Jaipur blasts in the context of Bangladeshi immigrants. She appears to be a dictator in the making. The need to be in the limelight often leads some inexperienced politicians to make a fool of themselves. Raje should learn her lessons or else the BJP central leadership should seek an alternative to her.

— S. Kamat

Goa

Meekly, in the end

• Pratap Bhanu Mehta's 'Too many reservations', teaches the unfortunate lesson that violence is often necessary to get attention. Before Independence, it used to be said that violent people are unfit for freedom, but if they are quiet then they don't need freedom. A basic premise of management is examining the relative merits of conflicting viewpoints in case of a dispute. Accordingly, one must decide whether to make concessions or reject the demands made. It is suicidal to reject the demand initially, but later meekly surrender in the face of violence.

— P.S. Sundaram

New Delhi

Karnataka scaffold

• Although the BJP has emerged as the single-largest party in Karnataka, it hasn't managed a simple majority and the survival of its government will be at the mercy of independent legislators.

Since their support is so crucial for the government, in situations such as the one in Karnataka, such legislators tend to hold the government to ransom. Therefore, the real winners in the just-concluded assembly polls in the state are the independents. Those who prop up the BJP government can look forward to reaping the maximum benefits of power.

— Hemant Kumar

Ambala

Fair play

• The Karnataka results demonstrate that Indian voters cannot be taken for granted. The people of Karnataka did not take the instability, that is, the betrayal by the JD(S) lightly. Thus they voted to preclude a repeat show by the JD(S) or anybody else. The governor should exercise his discretion judiciously and the BJP stand firm if the JD(S) and the Congress again try to form a coalition with the help of the independents. But with the likely support of five of the six independents, the BJP is near certain to form the government.

— S. Krishna Kumar

Dombilvi (East)

Heading: What’s left? - Indian Express
Content:
The Jaipur blasts have again focused attention on illegal migrants from Bangladesh. If migration is illegal, there is nothing wrong with the idea of deporting migrants and even sending them to transit camps in the interim. The 20 million (concentrated in West Bengal, Assam, Bihar, Delhi, Tripura, Rajasthan and Maharashtra in that order), if that is the right figure, shouldn't be deported today. They should have been deported long ago. One-shot attempts to legalise migrants who were historically illegal don't work, because the flow is never close-ended. There should be a difference between supporting (or opposing) migration and supporting (or opposing) illegal migration.

Migration occurs because of economic or non-economic reasons. In the Bangladesh context, Hindus (off and on), Chakmas and perhaps eventually Taslima Nasreen belong to the latter category. In the former category, there are both push and pull factors and one can understand why Bangladesh isn't very keen to curb migration. Remittances are not the only gain. If one asks around why Indians oppose illegal migration, the answers generally include security and terrorism, crime (distinct from security), employment threats to local population and threats to ethnicity, religion and culture. There may be instances (illegal organ trade, smuggling, terrorism) where one form of illegality has synergies with another.

But barring such examples, are these arguments against migration or against illegal migration? Since the beginnings of human history, people have moved in search of better opportunities. Our ancestors moved out of Africa 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. Till World War I, passports weren't quite required. There were controls, but those were typically controls to get into specific cities, not controls to get into countries. Hence, a passport did not mean a pass required to get into a "port". It meant a pass required to cross a "porte" or gate of a city. Before 1920, we didn't even have any kind of agreement on passports.

In 2005, India had a net migration of 1.4 million. That is, 1.4 million more people emigrated out of the country than came in through immigration. Using jargon, India had a negative net migration rate. The countries that had the largest positive migration rate were the United States, Afghanistan, Spain, Germany, Canada, UAE, the United Kingdom, Italy and Australia. Afghanistan is a special category and intra-EU migration sometimes has specific attributes. Having said this, what characterises these destinations or receiving countries is economic opportunities there, relative to sending countries. Not all migration is from developing to developed countries. But the largest sending countries are China, India and Philippines, in that order.

India's 1.4 million net figure is an annual flow. The stock of Indian migrants around the globe is 20 million. This diaspora estimate does not include second or third generation Indians. It is a figure of those who were born in India, but now live elsewhere. Not long ago, MOS for HRD scandalised every one by telling us that 38 per cent of doctors in the US, 36 per cent of scientists in NASA and 34 per cent of Microsoft employees are Indians. D. Purandeswari should have been more careful before making such statements in Parliament. Generally, such figures do not exist. To the extent they do, the Purandeswari figures are gross over-estimates. When India performed badly and messed up economic policies, capital flight took place. With some statistical question marks, there is now evidence that the reversal of capital flight has occurred. In a similar vein, good economic performance should lead to reversal of human capital flight. This has partly happened in IT, the financial sector and even higher education. Every time I meet a developed country academic who has opted (partly because of purchasing power parity considerations) to teach or do research in India, and the frequency of this seems to have increased, I am pleasantly surprised.

It will take a long time for India's net migration rate to turn positive. But the point is that it is a good sign if people want to migrate to India, just as it is a good sign for Maharashtra if people from Bihar wish to migrate there. We will know that sub-Saharan Africa's fortunes have changed the day a trend started 70,000 years ago is reversed, an argument equally valid for Bihar. If people from West Bengal begin to migrate to Bangladesh, one should seriously worry. Admittedly, employment and wage effects of migration on labour markets are not unambiguous. Overall efficiency and welfare gains do not negate temporary and sectoral (rickshaw pullers, construction, domestic help, brick kilns, farm labour, fishermen) unemployment and downward pressure on wage rates. Surely, the best response to security and criminal concerns is to encourage legal migration and tighten monitoring. Cross-border security is a concern even with countries where illegal migration isn't on such a large scale. For both crime and security, wouldn't a nation-wide biometric identity card help? Laxity in intelligence and policing should not always look for the scapegoat of illegal migration.

Why isn't more migration from Bangladesh legal? The answer has more to do with incentive structures than porous borders. There are little gains from legality and costs for legal migration are higher, which is where porous borders come in. On the Bangladesh side, costs (monetary and non-monetary) formulated by the Bangladesh Bureau of Manpower Employment are too high. This can be discussed bilaterally and even linked to

India's cross-border security concerns, provided we are clear that we wish to deport illegal migrants and replace it with an annual system of work-permit quotas. However, it is by no means certain that we wish to curb illegal migration. Ignoring acting presidents, who was the least memorable Indian president? I think Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed should win easily. But we should remember him for having recognised and perfected the use of illegal migrants in electoral strategy, at least in Assam, though this has since been replicated by both the Congress and the Left in other parts of the country. Consequently, expressions like "legal" and "illegal" are themselves dicey, since migrants who should be classified as illegal have electoral cards and ration cards. Therefore, there are no disincentives to illegality and, rather perversely, the Indian state apparatus encourages illegality.

This is perhaps best exemplified by the effective non-application of the Foreigners Act, 1946 to Assam and its replacement by the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunal) Act, 1983, or IMDT. In essence, IMDT makes detection and deportation of illegal migrants more difficult and places the burden of proof on the complainant rather than the migrant. The bottom-line is simple. Does India (not politicians) gain by sticking to the rule of law, or does India gain by deviating from it?

The writer is a noted economist

bdebroy@gmail.com

Heading: Life is elsewhere - Indian Express
Content:
Consider the first fallout of the Karnataka verdict. On Monday, the UPA-Left coordination committee meeting on the civil nuclear initiative was called off. The Centre's weariness of discussing with the communists the next steps in India's talks with the IAEA on nuclear safeguards is understandable. The Left has already begun demarcating the lines from which it feels the Congress strayed to bring upon itself this electoral setback. CPM General Secretary Prakash Karat says the verdict is a reflection on the Congress's credibility and the UPA's performance. His colleagues chime in with ample references to the Common Minimum Programme to make the point. To hear their glee, one could be forgiven for believing that the Left has actually achieved a hard-won victory. This is why a Congress spokesperson's question, post-Karnataka, strikes resonance: what have the Congress's allies done to improve its prospects?

There is no denying that the Congress ran its campaign in Karnataka most inadequately. But in going it alone, it had one idea right: the Indian voter is, in every state, now working on a two-alternative choice. If the Janata Dal (S) took away some of the "secular" vote, it is only because the Congress was less than artful in projecting itself politically. But for the Left to dissociate itself from the Congress's loss by citing the Central government's performance is disingenuous. This ruse by the Left of being both ally and adversary is at the heart of the UPA's problem. This way, the Left gets to own any initiative that works — like the NREGS, which is in actual fact a Congress-led idea. It also takes credit for obstructing the Congress-led UPA's autonomy to make economic and foreign policy. Yet, the Left tries to safeguard its ideological patch by running down the policies of the Congress. Therefore, not only is the UPA thwarted from governing as it may have, it is also held liable for the consequences of acquiescing to such pressure.

While both supporting the UPA government and chipping away at its credibility, the Left has been candid about its intention: to use political fragmentation to achieve its dream, a non-BJP, non-Congress third alternative. That multi-polar moment, as state election results from Uttar Pradesh to Karnataka show, passed a long time ago. The UNPA, the trial balloon floated as a nascent third alternative, has already shrunk. The AIADMK makes no secret of its affinity with the NDA, the DMK's kept away. The Samajwadi Party is showing openness to an alliance with the Congress. The Gowdas are discredited. Mayawati never took the UNPA seriously. The Left should introspect. Having hollowed out the terrain held by the Congress, it may itself have no way of occupying that space.

Heading: Let’s not control the essentials - Indian Express
Content:
Our reach must exceed our grasp or what's a heaven for? NASA's Phoenix lander has bits of Martian matter solidly in its clutch — and it has the world agog, waiting to know what it could imply, and whether centuries of speculation have any support. Ten years ago, NASA even began a programme in astrobiology: a mix of astronomy, geology and biology that is dedicated to the study of extra-terrestrial life — and an indication that it is not just cranks and dreamers, but also serious scientists who dedicate their careers to sketching such possibilities. There have been several mishaps on the previous 11 attempts, but Phoenix, which was assembled from the remains of a previous polar expedition, has proved to be a hardy little thing. It will scoop up and analyse samples of matter to ask the big question: could Mars support life?

Geological evidence and observation by other orbiters suggest that there might be vast amounts of ice hidden under the surface, which holds out possibilities of microbial life. But the crucial question is whether the ice melts, because "liquid water" is essential for incubating life. If there was a significant wet patch on Mars, that would lend credence to the idea that low-level life could exist on the planet next door. Or the wilder, grander hypothesis — that there might even have been more complex forms of life on Mars for a few million years, that died out, and meteors battered the planet for about 500 million years thereafter. Or perhaps, that microbial life originated in Mars and bits of rock, blasted by meteors actually made it to earth. Theories abound. Our appetite for them is the reason we are willing to foot the major costs of space exploration.

What explains our imaginative investment in Martiana, in little green men in their magnificent flying machines or in visions of colonising the red planet? The idea of a parallel world that we can make in our own image, or the idea that something alien could unwittingly reveal truths about our own situation? Whatever the reasons, neighbourhood visits rarely generate such excitement.

Heading: The anti-Al Qaeda wave - Indian Express
Content:
I usually have a trained economist's clarity on issues. But sometimes I am not sure. On Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays, I am in favour of strong Central governments. On Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays, well-run coalitions are not too bad. In the last 13 years, we have had five governments. They promise everything, but what is the economics dharma of a coalition? A good question, and it is perhaps the right time to ask it since we are not doing as badly as some bring it out to be. Twenty and a half million tonnes of wheat in the bin is not a joke.

Thank you, UPA. You did better than any government since the early '90s. If you give the kisan the right signals he will never let you down. Walking near Anand in the morning, I was struck by the sight of tractor trolleys. They had come to collect seeds from the agricultural university which got money after a long time from the Rajiv Gandhi Food Security Mission. But the good price of wheat was the turning point. We can do it again with rice. If we have wheat and rice in the bin, the latter selling in world markets at over Rs 40 per kg, and with foreign exchange reserves of over $300 billion, only stupidity will keep us from a 9 per cent annual inclusive growth.

The lessons for high growth are in fact quite simple. Prices are not just costs in women's household budgets and numbers in the wholesale price index. They efficiently ration scarce commodities and are also somebody's income. Don't control the essentials: energy, construction materials and food. Once, it made some sense when we gave powerful non-price signals for these, including investing government money in them. Now you are only mortgaging the not too distant future. Our industrialists will go and produce these more cheaply in foreign lands and we will have to do with expensive imports. The logic in the present dispensation is that competition and imports will take care of the market, the former by forcing efficiency and the latter by mopping up excess profits, if any, as compared to globally efficient costs. If there is evidence of somebody fixing markets, let a trained agency fix him. But don't do it at random. How much can we control anyway? A construction expert at the CEPT University, Ahmedabad, told us that the price rise in imported bathroom and other fittings, which is really high, contributes more to construction cost increases than materials. Is the imported tap to be turned off? With my personal income distribution preferences, it is a good idea, but not consistent with globalisation.

Energy has to be paid for. It is both inefficient and wasteful to subsidise imported fuel like we do. The only case is a subsidy for those living in hill areas so that they don't cut trees, but that is a small burden with a big payoff. A recent assessment of India's past by economic experts of the UPA looks at the '70s and '80s as very unfortunate periods in India's economic history, but energy management was much better then and it would be wise to have a more realistic energy policy. There is also the moral hazard of pensioner shareholders of the oil companies subsidising the economy at personal cost.

As an aside, if A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, M.N. Srinivasan and Anil Kakodkar, not to mention people like me, argue for the nuclear deal to be signed — we need at least a reasoned response, rather than obduracy. It is true that the government tends to side-step, if not oppose, the idea of completing the nuclear fuel cycle by following the thorium route, but the nuclear deal provides us with the means for reviving the case, which would languish otherwise in any case.

We need to withdraw wasteful purchasing power from the system to get back to a sensible interest-rate regime. Taxes, sensible prices and frugality, rather than waste, are like the mother-in-law. You can't have the good things of life without them. Reducing waste will permit more investment in infrastructure for which the time is right when world markets are wobbly. Restructuring is essential if the costs of globalisation are not to hinder progress. A higher growth rate is within reach. History does not treat has-beens well. We go from being the fourth-largest economy of the world to being the third or to the dustbin. The media have to describe the fork at which we are, so that choices are not made in ignorance. Those who would push us into ignominy must do so consciously and in the full glare of public scrutiny.

The writer is a former Union minister for power, planning and science, and was vice-chancellor of JNU, Delhi

yalagh@gmail.com

Heading: No longer held to ransom - Indian Express
Content:
After September 11, there was considerable fear in the West that we were headed for a clash of civilisations... But the religious leaders and former militants who are now critiquing Al Qaeda's terrorist campaign... make that less likely. The potential repercussions for Al Qaeda cannot be underestimated because... Al Qaeda's new critics have the jihadist credentials to make their criticisms bite. "The starting point has to be that jihad is legitimate, otherwise no one will listen, " says Benotman, who sees the Iraqi insurgency as a legitimate jihad. "The reaction [to my criticism of Al Qaeda] has been beyond imagination. It has made the radicals very angry. They are very shaky about it."

Why have clerics and militants once considered allies by Al Qaeda's leaders turned against them? To a large extent, it is because Al Qaeda and its affiliates have increasingly adopted the doctrine of takfir, by which they claim the right to decide who is a "true" Muslim. Al Qaeda's Muslim critics know what results from this takfiri view: First, the radicals deem some Muslims apostates; after that, the radicals start killing them. This fatal progression happened in both Algeria and Egypt in the '90s. It is now taking place even more dramatically in Iraq, where Al Qaeda's suicide bombers have killed more than 10,000 Iraqis, most of them targeted simply for being Shia. Recently, Al Qaeda in Iraq has turned its fire on Sunnis who oppose its diktats, a fact not lost on the Islamic world's Sunni majority.

Additionally, al Qaeda and its affiliates have killed thousands of Muslim civilians elsewhere since September 11...

Excerpted from 'The Unraveling' by Peter Bergen and Paul Cruickshank in The New Republic

Heading: Left Front to Buddha: be more cautious with land acquisition - Indian Express
Content:
Basudev Yadav, the 70-year-old who 'pioneered' the kidnapping industry in Bihar, surrendered to the police last week. Two weeks earlier, his disciple, crime lord Bhagar Yadav, gave in too.

The surrender of these two criminals coincided with Nitish Kumar's two and a half years in office—on May 25, Kumar reached the half way mark. Apart from the sustained police pressure on these ganglords to give up or face the consequences, the talk is that they surrendered in the hope of furthering the political careers of their children. Both Bhagar and Basudev Yadav's sons contested in the assembly elections and lost.

The two ganglords—who made abductions a money-spinning proposition in the state—surrendered in the backdrop of the state witnessing a marked decline in cases of kidnapping for ransom. Cases of abductions of doctors, engineers and students have come down in Nitish Kumar's Bihar. Government figures show that between January and October 2001—when the RJD was in power—314 cases of kidnapping for ransom were recorded. It came down to 166 during the same period in 2006 and 74 in 2007 after Nitish Kumar took over.

According to the state police, kidnapping for ransom had acquired the form of an industry and fetched the criminal gangs a staggering Rs 250 crore. Investigations had revealed that it was a well-established network with the gangs enjoying political and police patronage. The industry even inspired Bollywood to come out with films like Apaharan that were based on the spate of abductions in the state.

After the change of regime in the state, the police have been under pressure from the top to improve the situation. Speedy trial of pending cases saw hundreds of criminals behind bars. Though the police still have a long way to go before they can put an end to the menace, the drop in such cases is a big relief to traders and professionals and has gone a long way in restoring safety and security.

But at the same time, cases of students like Ankit and Akash who have remained untraced for months after being kidnapped, continue to haunt the political leadership. In both the cases, however, police say there was no demand for ransom and the students might have been kidnapped for other reasons.

Kidnapping for ransom started in Champaran district in the early 80s and Bausdev Yadav was the man who started it. The Indian Penal Code had no provision to deal with kidnappings for ransom while dacoity and murder—which the gangs practiced—invited stringent punishment. Basudev then started lifting potential preys at gunpoint and hid them in the riverine area he controlled and extracted good money. Slowly, other gangs in the state picked up the idea and several crimelords-turned-elected members used their privileged status to earn huge amounts by kidnapping businessmen, doctors and engineers.

Heading: Bengal flip complete: English-medium sections now in Bengali schools - Indian Express
Content:
The Left Front on Tuesday unanimously approved Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee's move to go ahead with industrialisation but urged the CM to move cautiously while acquiring land for industry. The message was conveyed to the CM during a brief meeting of the Front on Tuesday, the first after the recently-concluded panchayat polls.

During the meeting at the CPI(M) state headquarters here, RSP and Forward Bloc leaders highlighted the "manner" of land acquisition in Singur and Nandigram as the primary reason for the front's defeat. But CPI(M) leaders, including state secretary Biman Bose, reminded their allies that industrialisation was an integral part of Left Front manifesto for the 2006 Assembly elections.

Bhattacharjee, who was also present, reportedly accepted that there was some confusion among the people regarding land acquisition and industrialisation. But the CM said his Government could not give up its agenda as only industrialisation could change the quality of life in Bengal.

"We have decided that the state Government will move cautiously regarding land acquisition," said Bose. But RSP leader Kshiti Goswami warned: "If land acquisition goes on this way and with the present haste, it will harm the Left vote bank permanently."

CPI(M) sources said resistance had developed among locals against land acquisition and the party was gearing up to convince them. "No land acquisition will take place without convincing the affected people," said Bose.

Bose said caution always bears fruit. "We have seen it in Shalboni, Purulia and Salanpur in Burdwan," Bose added. "Industrialisation is an advanced thought. A backlash is obvious if we fail to convince the locals in our feudal society. So we told the Government to be cautious," he said.

CPI(M) sources said 'go-slow' strategy had also been necessitated by the general elections scheduled for next year. "We do not want to be hasty at this critical juncture. The panchayat results have opened our eyes. Local party committees are being told to organise camps wherever necessary to convince the people regarding the benefits of industry," said a senior party leader.

IN THE PIPELINE

• The Government has already issued a notice for acquiring 500 acres for its ambitious shipyard project at Geokhali near Nandigram, where the Left front had been wiped out in the recent local body polls

• Acquisition is also needed for the Kukrahati-Rajarhat Expressway and for the proposed chemical hub in and around Haldia

Heading: MP seeks Maharashtra help to store wheat surplus - Indian Express
Content:
Five years after it reintroduced English in Class I, the West Bengal Government took a radical decision on Tuesday to offer it as a medium of instruction in all government Bengali-medium schools.

The proposal was mooted by Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee and included in the agenda for the state Cabinet meeting. The CM was firm that this was needed to improve communication skills of Bengali students.

In 1984, in a controversial move, the state had abolished English from the primary section in all Bengali-medium government and government-aided schools. Following vehement protests from all quarters, English returned to Class V in 1992, Class III in 1998 and finally in 2003, it was decided that it would be taught from Class I onwards.

Bhattacharjee now wants to introduce English-medium sections in Bengali-medium schools. Starting this academic year, these would be introduced in Class I and Class XI. Next year, English-medium sections would be set up in Class II and Class XII.

There have been some protests, notably from PWD Minister and senior RSP leader Kshiti Goswami, who objected to the matter being placed before the Cabinet "in such an arbitrary manner". "There have to be talks with teachers' organisations, there has to be a discussion in the Left Front, and only then it can be placed for Cabinet approval."

A note by the School Education Department had commented on the mushrooming of private schools of poor standard and uncertain quality in the state, which were cashing in on parents' desire to send their wards to schools which offered English-medium.

"Guardians of students studying in private English-medium schools, who pay through their noses for the education of their kids, ask us why even though we have large government schools we could not arrange for English-medium sections. Their complaint is quite justified," said Partha Dey, Minister for School Education. In the first year a total of 120 schools have been earmarked for the new sections.

Heading: HRD Ministry asks NMC’s views on quota for Dalit Christians, Muslims - Indian Express
Content:
Madhya Pradesh's aggressive procurement of wheat, driven by the desire to reduce dependency on the Centre in the election year, has saddled it with so much stock that it is knocking on the doors of Maharashtra to store the surplus grain.

The Government has paid Rs 1,058 crore to farmers in procuring about 19.28 lakh MT of wheat — last year's procurement was less than 50,000 MT — since the procurement began on March 1 at 925 centres across the state. There are clear instructions not to send farmers away, so the procurement will go on for more time, probably till it rains.

Farmers are obviously happy because the state is paying them Rs 100 in bonus over the MSP of Rs 1,000. But in its zeal to procure as much as it can, the Government had failed to book private warehouses, which are not available now. The state can store only 11 lakh MT in its godowns and the FCI's capacity is hardly 4.2 lakh MT. FCI sources said even after hiring private godowns, their capacity won't exceed 6 lakh MT.

Wheat is lying in the open at some places because rakes are not available for transportation. The state's biggest worry is that unseasonal rains and early monsoon could play a havoc. The distribution of this wheat will begin only from July 1.

For the first time, collectors have been empowered to acquire private places to store the grain. "We have written to the FCI to allow us to send the surplus to Manmad in Maharashtra," commissioner of food and civil supplies K P Singh told The Indian Express on Tuesday. He said private godowns could store up 25 lakh MT but most of them were already booked.

If procurement continues at the present rate, the state will be left with at least 4 lakh MT surplus stock. Besides the FCI and the state civil supplies corporation, Markfed is also involved in procurement. Unlike last year when different agencies were allotted districts, there are no restrictions this season, one of the reasons why procurement was fast and in large quantities.

The state requires about 20.3 lakh MT wheat for schemes like PDS and mid-day meal. Obviously, the state would like to keep at least that much within the state because that was the basic idea.

An FCI official said the corporation could transport the surplus wheat to southern states but the state Government would have to take the call. "Since MP is the only state to have paid Rs 100 in bonus, it will have to come out with a clear policy on where to transport the surplus," he said.

Heading: Don’t be wary of offset clause: Antony to defence manufacturers - Indian Express
Content:
Though already neck-deep in quota quagmire, the HRD Ministry has now asked the National Minorities Commission (NMC) to present its assessment on the controversial issue of granting Scheduled Caste status to Dalit Christians and Muslims.

The NMC had recently commissioned a study which came up with strong recommendation for granting SC status for Dalit Muslims and Christians on the lines of Dalit Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists.

The HRD Ministry has also asked the NMC to take up the case with the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment which had earlier expressed some reservations on the issue, saying it would affect the 15% quota for Dalit Hindus.

Interestingly, "quota-friendly" HRD Minister Arjun Singh had made this move when the Government was resisting the pressure from coalition partners like the DMK, Ram Vilas Paswan's Lok Jan Shakti Party and Lalu Prasad Yadav who had made similar demands. They had been asking the Government to place the report by the National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities (NCRLM) Commission before the Parliament which had made similar recommendations on the issue of granting SC status for Dalit Christians and Muslims.

Paswan and Lalu had argued that it would help in taking on Mayawati as it would split her Dalit vote bank as the Hindu Dalits unwilling to share the reservation pie are against it. Both leaders had even taken up the issue with the Prime Minister, who is understood to be "hesitant" in creating yet another reservation controversy.

The study initiated by the NMC had looked into the contemporary status of Dalit Muslims and Dalit Christians in terms of their material well-being and social status. It had categorically stated that there was a strong case for including Dalit Muslims and Dalit Christians in the Scheduled Caste category.

"There are compelling arguments in favour of such an inclusion based on principles of natural justice and fairness. The balance of pragmatic considerations is also in favour of their inclusion. According due statutory recognition to Dalit Muslims and Dalit Christians would not only right a wrong, it would also remove an indefensible anomaly in our politico-legal system that can legitimately be construed as discriminatory," the study said. "In most social contexts, they are Dalits first and Muslims and Christians only second."

Heading: Pak must apologise for violating ceasefire: ministry - Indian Express
Content:
India has allayed fears of international defence manufacturers on its offset clause for military procurement saying it was a "bridge" between the industry and potential vendors to help private foreign players obtain licenses for joint manufacture of goods.

In his speech at a reception hosted in his honour here on the eve of Berlin Air Show, Antony said the procurement policies have been streamlined and were "transparent".

The policies have been put in place, including the requirement of an offset of 30 per cent, for certain contracts. This would act "as a bridge between the Indian defence industry and potential vendors, both foreign and Indian, to help private industry to obtain industrial licenses for the manufacture of defence products," Antony said.

Under the offset clause, companies getting any defence tender will have to source nearly 30 per cent of contract from India. However, a company securing a contract for 126 fighter planes will have to source 50 per cent under this clause.

The statement from the Minister came at a time when some companies have been talking in private of their inability to meet the 50 per cent clause of offset.

"These policies are designed not only to further develop our capabilities in production of land, air and naval defence equipment, but also to encourage co-development and co-production with international manufacturers," Antony said at the function attended among others by his German counterpart Franz Josef Jung and Air chief F H Major.

The Minister, who is here to attend the prestigious Air Show, where India has been chosen as the partner country, a first in the event's 99-year-old history, sought active role for private sector in its multi-billion dollar defence industry.

"The Indian defence industry, which has been largely in the state sector, has developed broad-based capabilities. We have recently put in place policies and initiatives to encourage private sector participation," Antony said, adding the defence sector in India was now open up to 100 per cent for Indian private sector participation, while foreign direct investment is permissible up to 26 per cent.

The Minister drew attention to the "enormous potential" in the sector as India "seeks to encourage active indigenisation in defence production as well as greater investment in research and development".

Heading: Susairaj confession recorded - Indian Express
Content:
Indicating a toughening of stance, the Defence Ministry has termed the recent violations of ceasefire along the Line of Control by Pakistani troops "unpardonable" and has called for an apology from Islamabad if it doesn't have "valid reasons" to explain the cross-border firing incidents.

Speaking to reporters at the sidelines of a CII-sponsored defence function in the capital the Minister of State for Defence MM Pallam Raju expressed surprise over the violations, one of which led to the death of an Indian soldier in the Medhar sector. "After five years of ceasefire, an untoward incident like this is unpardonable. If they don't have a valid explanation, I'm sure they will apologise at the appropriate forum," said the minister.

At a recent flag meeting in the Medhar sector, India registered a strong protest with Pakistan about the three incidents, which took place within the past month. The matter was also raised by External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee during his Islamabad visit.

While Pakistan has denied the involvement of its troops in the cross-border firing, the Indian contention is that any fire coming from across the border is the responsibility of the Pakistani army.

Meanwhile, Pallam Raju said that the army is anticipating an increase in infiltration in Jammu and Kashmir in the coming months as the snow in the high passes has begun melting with the advent of summer. However, he said that "adequate security measures" are being taken to ensure that this does not impinge upon the election process in the state.

Heading: Women outnumber men in J&K voter lists, inquiry ordered - Indian Express
Content:
In an important development in the sensational Neeraj Grover murder case that could strengthen the Mumbai Police Crime Branch's case against arrested accused Kannada movie actress Mariah Monica Susairaj (27)and her Naval officer boyfriend Emile Jerome Mathew (25), the first part of a confessional statement given by Mariah was recorded before a magistrate on Tuesday. According to Crime Branch officials, Mariah expressed a desire to give her confession on Sunday night, following which the police filed an application in court on Monday.

"On Sunday, Mariah expressed her desire to us that she wanted to give a confessional statement in court. The next day, we filed an application in court for the same purpose. From police custody, she was taken into judicial custody today, and a part of her confessional statement was recorded under Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code before a magistrate," said Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime) Rakesh Maria.

The confession was recorded before a chief metropolitan magistrate.

"Such a confession will bolster our case. One part of her confession was recorded today, and another part will be recorded either tomorrow or the day after depending on what the court decides. In this case, we want to file a chargesheet within 30 days and not 90, so that the case can come up for hearing faster," said Maria.

Susairaj and Mathew were arrested on May 21, for their alleged roles in the murder of Grover (25), who was a top executive at Synergy Adlabs and a former creative head at Balaji Telefilms. According to the police, Mathew stabbed Grover and then cut his body into small pieces that were placed by Susairaj in three bags.

The duo drove to Manor in Thane (Rural) carrying the bags, and after reaching an isolated spot there, poured petrol on the bags and set them on fire.

While the Crime Branch has managed to recover the bread knife with which Mathew allegedly cut Grover's body into pieces, they have not been able to trace the kitchen knife with which he allegedly stabbed him.

"We are still on the lookout for the kitchen knife with which Grover was stabbed. Mathew claims that he had placed it, along with the bread knife in one of the three bags that were burnt in Manor. We have recovered the bread knife, but are still on the lookout for the knife with which Mathew stabbed Grover.

Since the post mortem report has not ascertained the exact time of Grover's death, we do not yet know which of the two knives is the actual murder weapon, and both will be regarded as such.

All evidence that can be collected, included the murder weapon, bears weight in such cases," said Deputy Commissioner of Police (Detection) Deven Bharti.

Heading: Congress in huddle after Tura defeat - Indian Express
Content:
As Jammu and Kashmir prepares for Assembly elections later this year, discrepancies in the voter lists has come to light. In some segments, the number of women voters has been shown more than male voters, in contrast to census figures. A probe has been ordered.

This anomaly pertaining to around six-eight segments across the state was noticed during a review of electoral scene of the state.

It is in the Leh and Kargil district where the figures have shown unreal gender ratio in the voter list. The gender ratio at far-flung area of Zanaskar is also reported to be quite high. Interestingly, the highest gender ratio has been found in the Pulwama segment of south Kashmir.

In the Leh segment, for instance, as against the census figure of 823 (sex ratio), the gender ratio has been found at 977. Likewise in the Kargil segment, while the census figure is 837, the voter list mentions 1,014 in terms of gender ratio.

Other segments with such deviations are Nobra in Ladakh, Vijaypur, Suchetgarh, Akhnoor, Chhamb, Samba and Bishnah in Jammu region and some parts in Kashmir valley like Pulwama and Pampore. While the authorities concerned are looking into each and every aspect of the voter list, Chief Election Officer of the state BR Sharma has ordered a probe at block levels to find out the possible reasons for the discrepancies.

"We are having a relook at the figures and the formal findings will certainly lead us to some conclusions," said Sharma.

Heading: Kaziranga tiger cub killed by pesticide - Indian Express
Content:
After a string of defeats in the Assembly and Tura Lok Sabha bypoll, the state Congress has gone into a tizzy and initiated action to revamp its party units before the next Parliamentary election.

Meghalaya Pradesh Congress Committee (MPCC) president O L Nongtdu told The Indian Express on Tuesday: "We have sent circular to all the units at block level to go on an enrolment drive and strengthen the party as preparation for the next year's parliamentary election."

Nongtdu said election to the Congress block level should be completed by July 31. Revamping of the party at the district level would take place only after the All India Congress Committee (AICC) issued a circular to the Meghalaya Pradesh Congress Committee. "We will strengthen and revitalise all the party units and be ready for the Lok Sabha election next year," he said, adding the MPCC would meet soon to discuss and analyse its defeat in the Tura Lok Sabha by-election.

A senior Congress legislator said, "The Congress was defeated by 99,856 votes which does not give the party much hope of giving a fight in the next Lok Sabha election."

With former Chief Minister SC Marak refusing to fight the Tura bypoll, the ticket was given to former Meghalaya Minister Zenith A Sangma who had failed to retain his Assembly seat in March Assembly election.

Many Congress legislators feel if the Congress had fielded a better candidate than Zenith A Sangma it could have given the NCP a fight.

"We are yet to recover from the Assembly defeat and now we are experiencing another shock," said senior Congress legislator and spokesman Roytre C Laloo, adding the party needed to discuss in detail the steps required to set its house in order.

Heading: IAF’s cross-border airlift for China and Myanmar its largest ever - Indian Express
Content:
The Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) in Guwahati has confirmed that pesticide caused the death of a tiger cub in a tea estate near Kaziranga National Park in January this year.

According to R P Gohain, director of the FSL, lab tests found pesticide residues in the carcass the tiger cub had eaten before its death in the Rongagora division of Hatikhuli, a tea estate owned by Tata Tea Ltd. "We have found quite a high concentration of pesticide in the cattle carcass on which the tiger cub had fed," Gohain said.

A second tiger cub that also consumed part of the carcass survived and is currently lodged in the Centre for Wildlife Rehabilitation and Conservation at Kaziranga.

Meanwhile, Kaziranga National Park director S N Buragohain said that a case has been registered with the police under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, and that investigations into the incident are on.

"If the forensic laboratory has confirmed that the cub died due to pesticide consumption, then it is a serious matter. I hope the police will proceed with the laws accordingly," Buragohain said.

Incidentally, Kaziranga has the highest concentration of tigers anywhere in India. While the latest count conducted in 2001 had put the tiger population here at 86, the number must now be closer to 100, speculates Dibyadhar Gogoi, divisional forest officer (DFO) of the national park.

Heading: Army chief confirms survey in Sikkim’s Finger Area - Indian Express
Content:
The ongoing relief operations to China and Myanmar are the largest ever cross-border airlift effort by the Indian Air Force (IAF) with transport aircraft already hauling over 277 tonnes of relief materials to the disaster struck countries. Medium and heavy lift transport aircraft of the IAF have made over 14 trips to both countries this month carrying medicines, tents, sleeping bags, blankets, ready to eat meals and even an Army medical team.

"We are at present carrying out the largest ever across the border disaster relief mission to help our neighbours Myanmar and China in the aftermath of the cyclone and severe earthquake respectively," IAF spokesperson Wing Commander Mahesh Upasani said. While another IL -76 aircraft of the IAF will carry 28 tones of relief material to Chengdu on Wednesday, the Air Force has airlifted 152 tonnes of tentage, blankets, medicines and water purifiers to the country. This even surpasses IAF's foreign relief effort during the 2004 Tsunami disaster. For Myanmar, the IAF deployed both IL-76 and An-32 aircraft to carry critical supplies to Yangon.

Heading: BJP to play up its ‘biggest party’ card - Indian Express
Content:
Confirming that India was conducting a survey of the Finger Area in northern Sikkim that had been claimed by China, Army Chief Deepak Kapoor asserted that the region falls within Indian territory and "we can do survey and patrolling (in the area) as we have been doing it for years".

While the Army Chief said surveys were a "normal exercise", Minister of State for Defence M M Palam Raju said India and China were responsible neighbours and would bilaterally sort out any border-related issues.

"We have a strong neighbour in China. As responsible neighbours, if there is any issue we will sort it out," the minister said.

General Kapoor, however, sought to downplay the issue by saying this was not unusual as "we are carrying out such exercises in other places". "Surveys are normal exercises. Surveys along the border are continuing at a lot of places," he added.

As first reported by The Indian Express, China had staked a claim to the finger point, which is the northern-most tip of Sikkim, and had even planned to construct a road through the area.

Heading: JDS blames Cong for loss, to focus on LS polls - Indian Express
Content:
The Bharatiya Janata Party will use the coming national executive meeting to flaunt its recently-acquired status of the "biggest party in the country". After the recent victory in Karnataka, party president Rajnath Singh spoke about the party's newly-acquired "pan-Indian character". He'll use the two-day meet on June 1 and 2 to dwell on the "social, geographical and political" expansion of the BJP, once dismissed as a "Hindi-Hindu-Hindustan phenomenon".

The BJP is the ruling party in seven states today — Karnataka, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttarkahand and Chhattisgarh. The party also runs coalition governments in five states — Bihar, Orissa, Punjab, Nagaland and Meghalaya. The BJP is thus a stakeholder in as many as 12 states today, as against the Congress's 11— an all-time high for the main opposition party.

After tasting power in the SVD (Sanyukt Vidhayak Dal) governments in 1967, and the subsequent massive push forward during the JP movement, resulting in three chief ministers in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh in the form of B S Shekhawat, Kailash Joshi and Shanta Kumar, the BJP attaches great value to the latest win "that helped it surpass the Congress in terms of the number of states governed".

The BJP now hopes the party's Karnataka victory will boost its prospects in the four states going to polls this year — Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Delhi — apart from opening its account in states like Kerala.

The BJP-ruled states account for 206 Lok Sabha seats, but the party faces its greatest challenge in Uttar Pradesh which sends 80 members to the Lok Sabha. While UP is Rajnath's home state, general secretary Arun Jaitley, hailed as the man with the Midas touch in election-bound states, is the state in-charge. There are no indications, however, that the party is showing even a semblance of recovery in the state.

While "booth committees" played a huge role in the BJP's bid to win Gujarat for the second time in a row, the BJP president has made it a top priority in the party, with "two-thirds of booth committees" in place across the country. Rajnath will also highlight the move to reserve one-third of party posts for women.

Heading: Maha Cong revamp on, CM’s fate uncertain - Indian Express
Content:
Smarting over its debacle in the Karnataka Assembly elections, the Janata Dal Secular, following a meeting of 26 of its 28 MLAs on Tuesday, announced that it would now focus its energies on the parliamentary election "expected anytime soon".

While former prime minister H D Devegowda and his son former chief minister ducked out of interactions with the media following the meeting, party spokesperson Y S V Datta said the JD(S) had decided to work "this day onward" for success in the Lok Sabha polls. The spokesman said his party had not lost hope after its defeat, since it has suffered worse debacles in 1989 and 1999. The loss will be used as a lesson to return to the grassroots and rebuild the party, he said.

Blaming the Congress for the emergence of the BJP in Karnataka, Datta said the Congress had focused more on finishing the JD(S) rather than fighting the BJP. The BJP could have been kept out of power if the Congress had not spurned overtures made by the JD(S) for a re-alliance after it withdrew support for the BJP Government in November 2007, he said.

Reacting to Railway Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav's remark that Devegowda was responsible for the strength gained by the BJP in Karnataka, Datta said the RJD chief "has not seen the ground realities in Karnataka, and the remarks are based on his preconceived notion about the former Prime Minister".

The JD(S) legislators on Tuesday decided to hold further consultations on June 14 and 15 to study the causes for its loss. Though Kumaraswamy is the "undisputed leader" of the legislature party, a formal process of election will be held on June 15, Datta said.

The Congress is scheduled to hold a meeting on May 28 to take stock of its position following the election loss and for the selection of a leader for the Assembly.

Meanwhile, the new BJP government is expected to be sworn in on May 30. A sixth Independent MLA, who was not part of the five who vouched unconditional support for the party on Monday, has also been accepted as a supporter of the BJP. R Varthur Prakash, a Congress rebel from Kolar, had stated on Monday that he was in favor of a Congress-JD(S) alliance with his political guru and Congress leader Siddaramaiah as the Chief Minister.

Heading: Plan panel wants special authority for Bundelkhand - Indian Express
Content:
MaharashtraA Congress chief Prabha Rau looks set to go as the Congress high command got into the process of consultations on Tuedays over the party's revamp in the state. However, there was uncertainty over the fate of Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh as a dominant section of the central leadership continues to back him.

State Revenue Minister Narayan Rane, who has been gunning for Deshmukh citing his dismal performance, on Tuesday called on Congress president Sonia Gandhi and apprised her of the situation in the state. The high command was, however, non-committal on Deshmukh's fate, the party sources said. The search was on for Rau's replacement though, and party leaders Manikrao Thakre, Shivaji Rao Moghe and Eknath Gaekwad were said to be in the race for the PCC chief's post.

Meanwhile, several senior leaders at the party's central unit were learnt to be backing Deshmukh while blaming the state unit for not cooperating with his Government. They also argue that a change of guard in the state barely 16 months before the Assembly election could send out a wrong signal.

However, Deshmukh's detractors cited the results of the recent Thane Lok Sabha byepoll — won by the Shiv Sena— as an indicator of growing unpopularity of his Government.

While neighbouring Gujarat had surplus power, Maharashtra continued to reel under power crisis. The incidence of suicide by farmers continued unabated. Delay in the implementation of Srikrishna Commission report into 1992-93 Mumbai riots was also perceived to have turned the minority community against the CM. "Yet the Chief Minister remains nonchalant. He seldom meets even MLAs, not to speak of party workers. If the high command does not intend to remove him, it should be spelt out clearly as the current state of uncertainty has paralysed both the party and the Government," said a senior party leader from Maharashtra.

Meanwhile, Karnataka PCC chief Mallikarjun Kharge and senior party leader Dharam Singh on Tuesday called on Sonia Gandhi to explain the reasons for the party's defeat in the recent Assembly elections. They reportedly attributed the party's loss to the division of secular votes and sympathy factor for BJP chief ministerial designate B S Yeddyurappa.

Heading: Maya seeks Central aid for her sarvajan schemes - Indian Express
Content:
Encashing on the inability of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh to draw a socio-economic development plan for their drought prone areas, the Centre has sought their support in creating an empowered authority for Bundelkhand. This authority will have the autonomy to monitor implementation of a special package for region and also execute development programmes.

The need for such an authority was put forward by former Cabinet Secretary and now Planning Commission Member B K Chaturvedi at a meeting called to decide the Plan outlay for Uttar Pradesh on Tuesday. The suggestion carries weight since he is not only the member responsible for the state but also chairman of the group set up by the Prime Minister to recommend strategies for economic development of UP.

The response came in the wake of the UP Chief Secretary's demand that since both Bundelkhand and Vindhyachal have lost potential to become agriculture-based economies, they were entitled to benefits available to states such as Uttarakhand.

Politically, the move has has significance since it will at least ensure that drought-stricken people of the region acknowledge Centre's initiative in redressing their problem.

The Centre has already set up a group on development strategy for Bundelkhand and its recommendations are at various stages of implementation. A revival of economic activity in the region can help secure a leadership place for Rahul Gandhi who has been raising the issue.

Many farmers have committed suicide in Bundelkhand over the last five months and the state has termed the Centre's economic package of almost Rs 3,000 crore unacceptable. Following Congress general secretary Rahul Gandhi's tour in the drought-prone region, the Centre has seriously begun to initiate moves to revive the region's economy so that the BSP Government does not gain mileage from it.

So, the Congress, through the Planning Commission, is talking of creating an empowered authority to ensure that the Centre gets direct mileage for it.

Heading: Amar’s theory: BSP helped BJP beat Cong - Indian Express
Content:
Mayawati, who romped to power in Uttar Pradesh with massive support from the upper castes, now wants the Centre to foot half the bill for social welfare schemes aimed at consolidating her 'sarvajan' drive.

As part of the Annual Plan discussions with the Planning Commission, the Uttar Pradesh Government has demanded that the Centre bear 50 per cent of the expenditure on the scholarship scheme for general students from the pre-matric and post-matric classes. The Rs 450-crore scheme was launched after Mayawati came to power. She also wants 50 per cent Central assistance for the scheme to give coaching to general students for various exams. The anticipated expenditure for this scheme is Rs 13.50 crore for the current fiscal year. The CM also wants similar assitance for the grant extended by the state towards marriage of girls and medical treatment to families below the poverty line.

However, the Planning Commission, which finalised the annual allocation for UP on Monday, is dithering on these demands and has referred it to the Central ministries concerned. "These schemes came up for discussion between the state Government and the Planning Commission at the working group level," acknowledged UP Chief Secretary Atul Gupta. Though Gupta refused to elaborate, UP officials confirmed that the Commission has only referred the matter to departments concerned.

In fact, Mayawati's schemes are likely to put the UPA Government in a spot. With the Centre already in Mayawati's line of fire over the Uttar Pradesh package, she can once again blame the Congress for refusing to fund her schemes.

In fact, the Planning Commission, which approved an annual allocation of Rs 35,000 crore for the state, refused to grant Rs 5,000-crore additional assistance for different programmes citing the need for further consultations.

Heading: N-deal: Cong readies for final showdown - Indian Express
Content:
Days after the Congress suffered a major electoral jolt in Karnataka, the Samajwadi Party, in an apparent attempt to further mend its fences with the ruling party, claimed the BSP had played the role of BJP's "B-team" to thwart Congress' chances.

"Advani and Mayawati are working in collaboration. The outcome of the Karnataka election is a clear result of the tacit understanding between the two. This is part of an attempt to get either Advani or Mayawati as the next Prime Minister. BSP is playing like BJP's B-team," alleged Samajwadi party general secretary Amar Singh.

Adding that it was the BJP, which joined hands with the BSP in the past to thwart SP chief Mulayam Singh Yadav's chances of becoming Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister, Singh claimed the two parties were acting in tandem to thwart the Congress' chances in the next elections, with BSP dividing the votes. Incidentally, the BSP, which had dented Congress chances in Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh, was not able to eat into Congress votes in Karnataka.

Singh also said that while the BJP Government has allowed the BSP leader to organise a rally in Rajasthan on May 29, it did not allow Mulayam Singh to enter Bayana to express his solidarity with the protesting Gurjjars.

However, Singh denied any formal proposals from the Congress to join forces. In fact, he reiterated that the SP remains firmly with the Left parties despite "differences" over the Women's Reservation Bill". Singh, who had earlier said his party may "consider" its stand on the nuclear deal if the Government shared more facts, said the Centre has yet not given it more details.

Meanwhile, SP chief Mulayam Singh Yadav and Amar Singh held a closed door meeting with CPI(M) leaders Prakash Karat and Sitaram Yechury at the CPI(M) headquarters on Tuesday. Emerging from the meeting, Singh termed his party a "natural ally" of the Left asserting that all was well with their ties with and there was unanimity on most issues. Left leaders also toed the same line saying the meeting had helped both parties clear misunderstandings. The SP leaders had held discussions with CPI leader A B Bardhan recently.

Heading: UPA partners clash over modalities as panel takes up Women’s Bill - Indian Express
Content:
With the Left making noises about reviewing support to the UPA Government regardless of the Indo-US nuclear deal, there is growing restlessness in the ruling Congress camp about the need to take a final call on the deal.

Many top Congress leaders are of the view that since abandoning the deal is no guarantee for the Left's support till the end of the Government's tenure, it should think of going ahead with the deal that could be showcased as a UPA achievement in securing energy security for the country and providing power to farmers.

There are also indications that Prime Minister Manmohan Singh desires to express himself on the deal and to this end a high-level meeting of officials involved in negotiations could be held shortly. Indian Ambassador to the US Ronen Sen who was here recently was also learnt to have conveyed to the Government the urgency to take a final decision on the deal.

"A meeting may be convened to take a look at the available timeline for the deal so that if the Government, at some stage, has to bite the bullet, it should have a plan ready," said a ruling party source. The UPA-Left committee on the nuclear deal is likely to meet on June 11.

The CPI, RSP and Forward Bloc have already gone public with their intention to review support to the Government. Following the Congress's debacle in Karnataka, the CPI(M) has also taken a tough line, saying that the results reflect the UPA Government's performance. The four Left parties are likely to meet shortly to discuss this issue.

There is some thinking in the Left camp that it should not share the UPA's anti-incumbency by supporting the Government through its entire tenure.

Besides, as the Congress remains its main rival in its strongholds of West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura, the Left is wary of adding on to the anti-incumbency factor in these areas by sticking on to the UPA.

"The worst case scenario would be that we abandon the deal and then the Left withdraws support at some point of time. By going ahead with the deal, we will have at least something to talk about," said a senior Congress leader.

Heading: Defamation case: Sushil Modi apologises, let off - Indian Express
Content:
With the battle between supporters and opponents of the Women's Reservation Bill having shifted to the parliamentary standing committee, two important UPA partners clashed over modalities at the first meeting of the body on Tuesday. Notwithstanding these differences, the pro-Bill lobby managed to push the committee to draw a calendar for holding consultations and deliberations. This timetable, if followed, would make it possible for the committee to complete the process within the mandated 90 days.

Committee chairman E M Natchiappan told The Indian Express he and his colleagues would meet on June 3, 7, 10, 17 and 18. The Panchayati Raj Secretary has been called to give a presentation on reservation for women in panchayat bodies. The panel would visit Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai between June 23 and 28 to hear public views.

While Congress nominee Jayanthi Natarajan pleaded with the committee to study the Bill fast, Devendra Prasad Yadav of RJD, backed by Virendra Bhatia, Shafiqur Rehman Barq and Shailendra Kumar of Samajwadi Party, insisted that the panel do a thorough job. It was clear Congress, BJP and CPI(M) wanted to push the legislation and RJD and SP wanted to delay it by raising legal, Constitutional and procedural issues.

Natarajan's inclusion in the Standing Committee on Personnel, Grievances, Law and Justice was as interesting as it was sudden. Initially, Congress had got Mahila Congress chief Prabha Thakur on the committee after BJP nominated former Rajya Sabha chairperson Najma Heptulla to the body. The party, according to sources, chose to replace Thakur with Natarajan after realising that she would be no match for either Heptulla or Brinda Karat of CPI(M). Natarajan, for effective articulation and background of law, was considered a better bet.

Sources said Brinda and Natarajan reacted angrily when Tarlochan Singh (Independent) suggested the committee first study the performance of women members in panchayat bodies, where they enjoyed benefits of reservation. They sought to know if any such study had been conducted vis-à-vis male members.

Heptulla, reportedly very guarded during the meeting, raised a pertinent point: is there any reservation for OBCs in Parliament?

When Yadav, Bhatia, Shailendra Kumar and Tarlochan Singh suggested wider consultations and even visits by committee members to each state capital for the purpose, Najma, Brinda and Jayanthi all pointed out that the Bill had been pending for 12 years and it had already been discussed and debated enough. Yadav suggested the creamy layer formula, floated by the Supreme Court in the case of OBCs, be implemented vis-à-vis reservation for women.

He said the Bill overlooked the Constitutional provisions providing for "adequate representation" and advancement of people who are socially and educationally backward. He said the condition of women as such was not uniform. Terming the reservation of seats for women unprecedented, Verma advocated a global study to see whether it existed in any other country.

Heading: Author arrested for book on Ambedkar - Indian Express
Content:
Senior BJP leader and Bihar Deputy Chief Minister Sushil Kumar Modi was on Tuesday let off in a criminal defamation case by a court here for allegedly making slanderous remarks against a former advisor to the NDA finance minister after he offered a written apology to the complainant. Metropolitan magistrate Ravinder Bedi also asked Modi to pay damages of Rs 3 lakh to the Centre for Policy Alternatives and its chairman Mohan Guruswami.

Guruswami had filed a criminal complaint in 2004 against Modi, who as a Leader of Opposition in the Bihar Assembly had allegedly made defamatory remarks against him in a press conference. Guruswami in his complaint said Modi had defamed him by calling him corrupt and asserting that he had been removed from the Government on serious charges of corruption.

Modi's remarks, published in a national newspaper, prompted Guruswami to file a criminal defamation case against the leader and the newspaper's editor. While the editor was discharged earlier, the BJP leader approached the court and sought settlement in the case.

Heading: Court won’t stay wealth tax case against Jaya - Indian Express
Content:
A chapter in his yet to be launched book titled Ambedkarwaadache Khare Swaroop (Reality of Ambedkarism) which reportedly made certain comments on Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar landed Vijay Satpute in jail for a day.

The Meghwadi police booked him for "deliberately and maliciously outraging religious feelings by insulting religious beliefs" on the basis of a complaint lodged by Sumedh Uke on May 11. Satpute was taken into judicial custody and later released on bail.
