The two are interrelated, but it would be unwise to treat them as one, however comforting it is to blame the rest of the world for our woes. Incidentally a few weeks ago and for some even now, globalisation was all the good things of life. Maturity requires that the flip side is also recognised and provided for, since the global bazaar works fully and mercilessly both ways. The government is working on a strategy and it is interesting to think of its components since finally the price will have to be paid by workers, producers and consumers. We go back to earlier experiences since the devil is in the detail and much as we would like, there are no easy solutions. Some of the flamboyant gestures suggested, like asking Madam Gandhi to walk out of the coalition don't further the cause of nuclear energy one bit and also distract attention from serious possibilities being negotiated. Needless to say no two situations are the same and yet successful contours of the past should be of interest.

We know from the first energy crisis that a big jump in the energy price has a macro imbalance aspect. In the first energy crisis we walked on two legs. It was savage on energy prices, petrol becoming the most expensive in the world. In Delhi officers switched to car pools and contract buses and in Ahmedabad box cars were attached to scooters, as families put cars in mothballs and the demand for petrol actually went down. All this is unnecessary now since oil imports met from reserves would in fact be deflationary, since oil purchased with dollars will be paid with rupee purchasing power, but scarcity prices have to be paid. The government is finally doing it and the cribbers will have to be exposed.

The more interesting part is the macro story. We should not accept lost years in inflation. That needs a technocratic map and a realistic negotiating strategy. It is obvious that the oil dollar effect is not deflationary enough. It would be very counterproductive to go slow on the rupee expenses on flagship schemes like the NREGS, the agricultural schemes and education and health. Something has to give. Working through interest rates is not enough and also inhibits investment. In the first energy crisis wages and profits were squeezed. It is not just the principle but the details which are important. The notion that the other fellow has to pay the price for inflation control (taxes cannot be raised) will not wash. If per capita income is rising by 7.5 per cent, prices can rise by 4.5 per cent, then all claims have at the margin to be less than 12 per cent, for the inflationary overhang has also to be neutralised. The details of "we will all pay for it" can provide a base for negotiation. In the first energy crisis it was Sukhomoy Chakravarti, backed by the Planning Commission boys working with the finance ministry and convincing the PMO. Energy prices have been raised in later coalition regimes, in 1996 and so on. We need a credible roadmap and then start negotiations in the framework of carrying the political process with it.

The notion that political parties will not bite is giving up without trying. It is true that reform without consensus building is impractical. But there are also too many instances of parties accepting the second best if not the optimal answer. The Left parties were against distribution privatisation in the electricity sector. They did not allow earlier bills to be tabled. But in the late nineties a parliamentary committee met through stages all their legitimate concerns on social control of grid management, supported by the then ministry by me and a Distribution Bill was unanimously approved. This was used to push through

India's largest and in fact only foreign investment in distribution of electricity. The draft bill was later incorporated in fundamentals into the Electricity Act. Political parties will react to slogans with slogans but since they represent interest groups, they have to react to detailed roadmaps with arguments.

Experts have recently highlighted the nuclear decision of the late Rajiv Gandhi, but it was a part of a holistic strategy of pushing non-proliferation globally, detailed cooperation with the USSR on the fast breeder reactors and the GSLV, with the US on strategic cooperation as also with France, Japan and Italy. With the USSR we not only negotiated the light VVR reactors and the cryogenic engines, but also laid economic relations on the fast track in the first round of reforms. The rupee was in the first basket of currencies traded in Russia and commodity trade was placed in this context by a group we chaired after the Rajiv-Gorbachev objective of "doubling trade". The Indo-US Technology Forum goes back to that period. The opposition to the nuclear agreement has to be surrounded in the blanket of national self-interest and all legitimate arguments on costs and national self-interest met by the external affairs minister's group so that no alternatives exist. Coalitions work harder so that there is no going back.

The writer is a former Union minister for power, planning and science, and was vice-chancellor of JNU, Delhi yalagh@gmail.com

Heading: Political realities - Indian Express
Content:
There is no doubt that a vast majority of the people living in India and Pakistan want peace , for a plethora of reasons — nostalgia, the shared culture, and the economic benefits which will accrue to both sides. Yet, there are very few who have thought in terms of structured philanthropy of any sort in the other's country.

There are various reasons for this. First, for most individuals it is near impossible to visit each other's country, so the question of charity is a far cry. Second, there are enough who visit the other's country and meet friends, shop and interact with the crème de la crème of society. So where is the time to think of any philanthropy. For many, what sense does it make to do philanthropy in the other's country — after all the blinkers of nationalism cannot vanish all of a sudden. Why blame residents from India and Pakistan, very few non-resident Indians, who are economically more sound and bereft of any political pressures, have thought of philanthropy in Pakistan and vice-versa.

Amid all the pessimism, hopes persist as a result of the efforts of groups like the International Punjabi Foundation — an Ontario-based group of diasporic Punjabis (of Indian origin) who have no blinkers of nationalism or faith. Members of this foundation have been holding free eye camps in Pakistan for the last three years and have held them in the towns of Nankana Sahib, Eminabad, Kartarpur . The last eye camp was held in 2007 in honour of Bhagat Singh and was named Shaheed-E-Azam Bhagat Singh Eyes Camp in Chak 105 Banga (District Faisalabad), Pakistan. In 2006 when the foundation ran out of money they held a gala evening, the proceeds of which went to the 2007 eye camp.

Individuals like those belonging to the International Punjabi Foundation have not lost sight of humanity, and if more people were able to think in terms of humanity and hold free eye camps, a lot of people's eyes would be opened both literally and figuratively.

Heading: Clinton takes Puerto Rico, but loses super delegates - Indian Express
Content:
•Shekhar Gupta is too polite in his analysis of the emerging electorate that is responding to globalisation through the breathtaking communication revolution that is sweeping across rural India 'The rurban mind'. The Congress, one of the two main national parties, is very casual not only in its understanding of the changes sweeping across what were hitherto villages and are now getting urbanised, but also in its response.

Incidentally, the difference between the Congress score and that of the BJP in 2004 was less than ten seats. Yet, the Congress is allowed to get away with the impression of more than what the party's achievement is.

— Prasad Malladi

Nidadavole

Congress's options

•I refer to your editorial 'Left with no time' where you asked, "Is the Congress ready to put India's nuclear interests above the political survival of UPA?" I think the political survival of the UPA has been already threatened rather than strengthened by the Congress-led government succumbing to the Left's pressure all the time.

The national mood is clearly in favour of the nuclear deal for peaceful uses. The Congress should revert to its original determination to fight the next general elections without the support of or any understanding with the CPM, which is undecided whether it should withdraw support on the issue of price rise or the nuclear deal.

Here is a golden opportunity for the Congress to end its alliance with the CPM, and forge one with Mulayam Singh Yadav's Samajwadi Party in UP, at least for the Lok Sabha elections.

— Parimal Y. Mehta

Mumbai

Burney issue

•The statement of regret issued by the home ministry on former Pakistan minister and human rights activist Ansar Burney's shocking deportation is unconvincing and inconsistent 'Burney bungle: A 16-yr-old notice lands India in spot'. It said that Burney was travelling on a SAARC sticker issued to ministers in SAARC countries so that they are spared the hassle of obtaining visas and it was not clear to the immigration officials whether he could be permitted to use the sticker after he had demitted office.

But the ministry has no answer to Burney's question as to how he was allowed entry with the same SAARC visa six weeks ago when too he was no more a minister in the Pakistan government.

— M.C. Joshi Lucknow

Be Warned

•The final of the first season of the Indian Premier League was entertainment all the way! If the seesawing fortunes of the teams had the spectators at the edge of their seats, the nail-biting finish ensured an apt finish for the grand finale. The topic of conversation, however, will long hover around the exploits of Shane Warne, the captain-cum-coach of the Rajasthan Royals. What Warne has achieved with a bunch of otherwise nondescript individuals speaks volumes about the cricketing acumen of an individual whose entire career was mired in controversies.

— Pachu Menon

Margao, Goa

Heading: A battered Sunday at Obama’s former church - Indian Express
Content:
Hillary Rodham Clinton won another overwhelming victory over Barack Obama on Sunday—this time in Puerto Rico—even as many Democrats, including some of her supporters, suggested it would be best if she dropped her threat to battle on past the end of the primary voting on Tuesday.

"There's nobody taking Hillary's side but Hillary people," said Donald Fowler of South Carolina, a former national party chairman and one of Clinton's most prominent supporters, referring to her campaign's suggestions that she might seek to challenge the way the party resolved the fight this weekend over seating the Michigan and Florida delegations. "It's too bad. She deserves better than this."

In a telephone interview Sunday from San Juan, Puerto Rico, Clinton still raised the possibility that she would challenge the party's decision on seating those delegates. "Well, we are going to look at that and make a determination at some point," she said. "But I haven't made any decision at this time."

Heading toward what is shaping up as something less than a triumphant moment of victory as the voting draws to a close, Obama spent Sunday in South Dakota for a last-minute schedule of campaigning. He was in the state, which will vote along with Montana on Tuesday to complete the primary season, trying to thwart a last-minute effort by Clinton to pull out a victory there and build her case that she would be the stronger candidate in the general election.

The dimensions of Clinton's challenge were underlined as two more superdelegates signed on to Obama.

Clinton won by 2 to 1 in Puerto Rico, where she seemed to revel in a weekend of campaigning even as her surrogates fought in Washington to keep her campaign alive.

The victory—coming among Hispanic voters, who are a key constituency in the fall election—underscored a constant source of frustration among Clinton and her supporters: that her strong finish over the past months, with big victories among blue-collar voters, have shown no signs of pushing uncommitted superdelegates into her camp.

"Most Clinton supporters are filled with bewilderment that this is happening," said Gov. Edward G. Rendell of Pennsylvania. "We are willing to go on, and we understand the inevitability of this, but we are filled with disappointment and amazement: Why haven't these results caused the superdelegates to come around?"

Clinton, in the interview, in a new television advertisement and in her victory speech in San Juan, laid out why superdelegates should rally around her. She argued that by the time the final vote is counted, she will have more popular votes than Obama, an assertion that has been disputed.

"I think it will be most likely the case in a few days," Clinton said from San Juan. "I will have won the most votes—more than anyone in the history of the primary process."

Heading: Louisiana champions Jindal as McCain VP - Indian Express
Content:
For weeks, the members of Trinity United Church of Christ on the South Side of the city felt battered by the national spotlight that had accompanied the growing fame of their longtime member, Senator Barack Obama.

First came the endless television coverage of incendiary statements by the Rev Jeremiah A Wright Jr, their controversial former pastor. Then reports of a visiting Roman Catholic priest who had mocked Hillary Clinton. And finally on Sunday, a day after Obama announced that his family was leaving the church, satellite trucks idling again outside the 7:30 am service.

Inside the packed sanctuary of more than 2,000, the Rev Otis Moss III, the new pastor, did not directly mention in sermons the political tumult surrounding the church. But in a flier that workers slipped into church programs, Moss commented at length about the situation, calling the decades-old Trinity a "new church being birthed in the crucible of a public moment."

"We, the community of Trinity, are concerned, hurt, shocked, dismayed, frustrated, fearful and heartbroken," Moss wrote to his members. "Our hearts break at this moment and my limited vocabulary is inadequate to describe the range of emotions flooding our spirits at this time. We are caught, it seems, in a strange Greek tragic-comedy. In the words of Jean Paul-Sartre, with 'no exit.' We are a wounded people and the bruises from our encounter with history have scarred our very souls."

Outside the church, many members brushed silently past reporters. Those who spoke said they were angry, mostly at the news media—for failing, they said, to take the time to fully study the words of Wright and the works of Trinity; for trying to tear down Obama, a beloved member of the church for almost two decades; and, most of all, for turning their private worship into a public spectacle. They said that they remained supportive of Obama and that they were saddened, but not angered, by his choice to leave the church under the relentless pressure.

The church issued a brief public statement on the Obama family's departure. "Though we are saddened by the news, we understand that it is a personal decision," the statement said. "We will continue to lift them in prayer and wish them the best as former members of our Trinity community."

One man, whose job it was to usher congregants across busy 95th Street toward the church, pointed toward a cluster of news cameras and said: "Watch out for the vultures. God bless them and move on." Even the salesman on a corner outside the church selling Obama T-shirts and caps refused to speak with reporters.

For Moss, who is in his 30s, Sunday was also a changing of the guard. Although Wright's formal departure as pastor into a role as "pastor emeritus" had been months in the making, Moss for the first time took the chief pastor's seat at the center of the sanctuary on Sunday.

In the flier handed out to members, a work he titled "The Declaration of Interdependence," Moss mentioned no names but alluded to the public conflict that had emerged between Wright and Obama, who has denounced Wright's controversial remarks. Wright preached Black Liberation Theology, an often fiery philosophy that argues that those who have suffered or been oppressed occupy a special place when it comes to faith.

Heading: As protests grow, Brown sticks to terror crackdown - Indian Express
Content:
Religion and fiscal stringency have a friendly home at the state Capitol here, with a conservative, Bobby Jindal, in the governor's office, a host of straight-arrow novice legislators eager to please him and an honoured spot for the Louisiana Family Forum in the old marble halls.

The newly conservative tone of state Government is seeping through a host of successful bills— on school vouchers, creationism, stem-cell restrictions and tax and spending cut— and it is adding to the speculative frenzy here surrounding Jindal as a potential vice-presidential choice for Senator John McCain.

Politicians here say they are certain that Jindal would balance a McCain ticket, and not just because he is an Indian-American. The Christian right has a new champion in Jindal, a serious Catholic who has said that "in my faith, you give 100 per cent of yourself to God."

Bumper stickers saying "Jindal for VP" are circulating here, with increased velocity after the governor's stay two weekends ago at McCain's Arizona ranch. McCain's schedule has him campaigning in Louisiana next week, according to his website.

"He has everything McCain is lacking," said State Representative John LaBruzzo, a Republican, speaking of Jindal. "He's seen as a true conservative, which McCain is seen as less than."

In the Legislature, the climate for a conservative Christian agenda is warmer than in years. Some of that agenda, including a school voucher programme for New Orleans that Jindal calls a "scholarship plan", is being pushed vigorously by the governor. On other parts, like a bill favoured by Christian conservatives that opponents say is a stalking horse for teaching creationism, Jindal has been well in the background, though legislators say they think the governor would sign it, as he has raised doubts about evolution.

On still other issues, like tax and spending cuts, the zealous young legislators have gotten ahead of the 36-year-old governor. Members of the State House of Representatives, following Jindal's campaign vows to rein in Government spending, cut some $240 million in health and education spending. Jindal now says he wants that money restored to his $30 billion budget proposal.

Meanwhile, the House is considering an income tax cut that would cost the state $300 million, an idea that did not originate with Jindal, though he has endorsed it.

Jindal's spokeswoman did not respond to messages on Friday.

On the floor of the House this year, several legislators have invoked the position of the Louisiana Family Forum, a faith-oriented, anti-abortion group that is affiliated with conservatives like James C Dobson of Focus on the Family and Tony Perkins, who helped found it. Its executive director, the Rev Gene Mills, has become a frequent presence in the legislative halls. At the group's modest offices here, Jindal is seen as practically one of the family.

Heading: Yves Saint Laurent, a giant of couture for 45 yrs, is dead - Indian Express
Content:
British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said on Monday he would stick to his principles over plans to detain terrorism suspects for longer prior to being charged despite the prospect of a humiliating defeat in parliament.

With a rebellion rumbling in the ranks of his ruling Labour Party and threatening Brown's faltering leadership, the Prime Minister said a plan to allow detention of suspects for up to 42 days without charge was the "right thing" to do "to protect the security of all and the liberties of each."

Brown, whose Labour Party lost a safe parliamentary seat last month and was beaten into third place in local elections, does not have to call a national election until 2010, when he hopes the economy will have had time to recover.

His poll ratings have fallen in recent months, wiping away the political "honeymoon" he enjoyed after taking over from former prime minister Tony Blair almost a year ago.

As many as 50 Labour parliamentarians are thought to be ready to vote against Brown's 42-day detention plan when it comes to the vote next week. The plans, which would extend the 28-day pre-charge detention limit, were attacked by the government's former top lawyer, ex-attorney-general Lord Goldsmith, who described them as a "very serious incursion on our fundamental freedoms."

Interior Minister Jacqui Smith was scheduled to meet the parliamentary party later on Monday to try to persuade them to fall into line behind Brown.

Writing in The Times newspaper, Brown said he would not give ground.

Political analysts say Brown will be fighting for his political life over the next two months and may struggle to survive as party leader into the summer parliamentary recess.

Heading: Mehsud flaunts power in Pak, angers US - Indian Express
Content:
Yves Saint Laurent, who exploded on the fashion scene in 1958 as the boy-wonder successor to Christian Dior and endured as one of the best-known and most influential couturiers of the second half of the 20th century, died on Sunday at his apartment in Paris. He was 71.

His death was confirmed by Dominique Deroche, a spokeswoman for the Pierre Bergé-Yves Saint Laurent Foundation.

During a career that ran from 1957 to 2002 he was largely responsible for changing the way modern women dress, putting them into pants both day and night, into peacoats and safari jackets, into "le smoking" (as the French call a man's tuxedo jacket), and into leopard prints, trench coats and, for a time in the 1970s, peasant-inspired clothing in rich fabrics.

Saint Laurent often sought inspiration on the streets, bringing the Parisian beatnik style to couture runways and adapting the sailors' peacoats he found in Army-Navy stores in New York into jackets that found their way into fashionable women's wardrobes around the world. His glamorous evening clothes were often adorned with appliqués and beadwork inspired by artists like Picasso, Miró and Matisse. Above all, he was a master colourist, able to mix green, blue, rose and yellow in one outfit to achieve an effect that was artistic and never garish.

Saint Laurent achieved instant fame in 1958 at the age of 21 when he showed his Trapeze collection, his first for Christian Dior following the master's death. But unlike many overnight sensations, Saint Laurent managed to remain at the top of his profession as fashion changed from an emphasis on formal, custom-made haute couture to casual sportswear.

For many years after he opened his own couture house, in 1962, his collections were eagerly anticipated by fashion enthusiasts, who considered his the final word on that season's style. His influence was at its height during the 1960s and '70s, when it was still normal for couturiers to change silhouettes and hemlines drastically every six months.

Among his greatest successes were his Mondrian collection in 1965, based on the Dutch artist's gridlike paintings, and the "rich peasant" collection of 1976, which stirred so much interest that the Paris show was restaged in New York for his American admirers. "The clothes incorporated all my dreams," he said after the show, "all my heroines in the novels, the operas, the paintings. It was my heart—everything I love that I gave to this collection."

By 1983, when he was 47, his work was recognised by fashion scholars as so fundamentally important to women's dress that a retrospective of his designs was held at the Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the first time the museum had honoured a living designer. Diana Vreeland, the legendary magazine editor and the doyenne of the Costume Institute, who masterminded the exhibition, called him "a living genius" and "the Pied Piper of fashion."

Heading: Nepal’s deposed king agrees to leave one palace, given another - Indian Express
Content:
With great fanfare, the Pakistani Army flew journalists to a rugged corner of the nation's lawless tribal areas in May to show how decisively it had destroyed the lairs of the Taliban, including a school for suicide bombers, in fighting early this year.

Then, just days later, the usually reclusive leader of the Pakistani Taliban, Baitullah Mehsud, held a news conference of his own, in the same region, to show just who was in charge.

He rolled up in an expensive-looking Toyota pickup packed with heavily armed Taliban fighters, according to the Pakistani journalists invited to attend. Squatting on the floor of a government school, Mehsud, clasping a new Kalashnikov, announced he would press his fight against the American military across the border in Afghanistan.

"Islam does not recognise boundaries," he told the journalists, in accounts published in Pakistani newspapers and reported by the BBC. "There can be no deal with the United States."

Mehsud's jaunty appearance in his home base, South Waziristan, a particularly unruly region of Pakistan's tribal areas, underscored the wide latitude Pakistan's government has granted the militants under a new series of peace deals, and its impact in Afghanistan, where NATO and American commanders say cross-border attacks have surged since talks for those peace deals began in March.

The impunity of Mehsud's behaviour has outraged the Bush administration, which is pressing the Pakistani government to arrest and prosecute him. "Bringing Baitullah Mehsud, the head of this extremist group in South Waziristan—capturing him and bringing him to justice, which is what should happen to him," is what the United States wants from Pakistan, Deputy Secretary of State John D. Negroponte said last month in testimony before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

But the Pakistani government, which at times has considered Mehsud an ally and is now fearful of his power, appears reluctant to hunt him down. Days before his news conference, Pakistani forces pulled back from his realm in South Waziristan as part of the peace deals.

American and Pakistani officials accuse Mehsud of masterminding the assassination of Benazir Bhutto, a former prime minister, in December and sending scores of suicide bombers here and in Afghanistan, while forging a symbiotic relationship with al-Qaeda on Pakistan's frontier.

He and his main ally, Qari Hussain, whom officials and associates have described as a highly trained and vicious militant, have methodically built up strongholds in North and South Waziristan—killing uncooperative tribal leaders, recruiting unemployed young men to their jihad and filling the vacuum left by a lack of government services. Now, they also have lieutenants and allies across the tribal region.

Local Pakistani authorities say they are helpless to deal with Mehsud's group. In a measure of their despair, on Wednesday the authorities in the Mohmand district, where the conference and public execution were held, announced a truce with the Taliban.

Mehsud was once a minor figure in the small Shabikhel branch of the fierce Mehsud tribe that lives in South Waziristan, whose inhospitable territory remained a sliver of imperial India left unconquered by the British. But he managed to enhance his stature through the ambivalence—or protection, according to some officials—of the Pakistani authorities, say former Pakistani military officials and tribal leaders. His strength grew quickly after February 2005, when the military, then under the control of President Pervez Musharraf, signed a peace deal with him.

"That was when I knew the army was not serious," said a tribal leader who has dealt with Mehsud and would not be named for safety reasons. "If the army took firm action they could crush him in two months." Instead, the army and the Inter-Services Intelligence, the overarching Pakistani intelligence agency, wanted to keep Mehsud "in reserve," said the tribal leader, who is also a former military officer.

In essence, the Pakistani authorities stuck to a long-standing policy of "strategic depth" in Afghanistan as a bulwark against its enemy India, and Mehsud was a tool in that game, he said.

Heading: Food summit to reflect on neglect of farming in poor countries - Indian Express
Content:
Gyanendra Shah who was ousted as the King of Nepal on May 28 through a legislative decree will be vacating the Narayanhiti Palace within the stipulated 15-day deadline.

The government, it is believed, will allott the Nagarjun Palace for his residential purposes. This palace too had been nationalised last year. This was communicated to Pashupati Bhakta Maharjan, who was the principal secretary to the former king, by Prime Minister G P Koirala.

Home Minister K P Sitaula separately met Shah at Narayanhiti palace on Monday. "He has accepted the decision of the constituent assembly and will be vacating the palace within the stipulated time," Sitaula told reporters after his meeting.

In the past two days, two different groups of the government have visited the palace. The first went to the palace on Sunday to make an inventory of the palace property. The second, by Sitaula today, was to discuss the former royal's exit.

Sitauala said that the former king was concerned about his security and alternative residence. "He has taken the development with grace." It is still not known what arrangements the government is going to make for former queen mother Ratna and the 92-year old Sarla, partner of late King Tribhuvan (grand father of Gyanendra Shah), who have been living in separate buildings within the Narayanhiti complex.

According to sources, there is some confusion over whether the government is to take over the entire complex or part of it since a chunk of the palace grounds belongs to the private trust of the Shah family. In the meantime, a petition was filed before the Supreme Court today challenging the validity of the procedure of the House of Representative that declared Nepal a republic on May 28. Some lawyers challenged the decision on the ground that the House which adopted the resolution was incomplete in composition as all the 26 seats belonging to the 'nominated category' were vacant, and secondly because, Home Minister K P Sitaula who moved the resolution on giving Nepal a republic status, had been defeated in the polls and he was not entitled to enter the Constituent Assembly.

The petition further pleaded that the resolution had been put up for voting and adopted without any debate being allowed on the motion.

Heading: ‘Dr Death’ Patel likely to file fresh bail plea - Indian Express
Content:
Ferried in by helicopters and boats or loaded on the backs of yaks and elephants, massive amounts of food aid have reached millions of homeless or hungry people after disasters in the last few years.

But while the world rises to the challenge of saving those survivors from starvation, hundreds of millions go hungry from a catastrophe that has stubbornly lasted for decades: the failure of agriculture in much of Africa and some parts of Asia and Latin America to ensure enough food for their own.

World leaders convening in Rome on Tuesday to grapple with skyrocketing food prices will have to make progress on this problem if they want to eradicate chronic hunger, say UN experts, nonprofit aid groups and economists.

As the recent outpouring of nearly $1 billion to help the UN purchase emergency aid during the current food price crisis might show, the world can be more willing to take on dramatic emergencies than to invest in helping poor countries to feed themselves.

"What we've seen is we're getting better at emergencies, but getting worse at tackling chronic hunger," said Duncan Green, director of research at Oxfam, a British aid group.

"Even in 2006, which was a good food (harvest) year, 850 million people were hungry," said Raj Patel, a political economist who testified earlier this month before Congress about the food crisis. "It's part of a chronic crisis which has recently become acute"because of soaring prices.

Agricultural development has been "horrendously neglected," Oxfam's Green said in a telephone interview from Britain before the June 3-5 UN summit in Rome. "I'd say it's three decades of neglect," said Jim Butler, deputy director-general of the U.N. Food and Agricultural Organization, which is hosting the summit. He said his agency will encourage aid to small farmers in the form of seed, feed, supplies, fertiliser and technology.

An internal report by the World Bank, which wealthy countries finance to help poor ones, concluded last year that the institution had long neglected farming in sub-Saharan Africa. US congressional investigators said last week that African-bound food aid, particularly from the United States, has increasingly been sent for short-term emergencies rather than to help long-term agricultural development.

"We tend to deal with what is happening now, today, tomorrow or next week, and insufficient attention is given to more fundamental processes such as population growth, or the need to invest in agriculture research for people living in difficult environments," said Timothy Dyson, an expert in agriculture and famine issues at the London School of Economics.

Heading: Syria invites IAEA to inspect ‘nuclear reactor’ site - Indian Express
Content:
The case of Indian-born surgeon Jayant Patel, arrested in America over death of 17 patients in Australia, is all set to be heard by a US court on Monday, which could see the defamed doctor filing a fresh bail plea.

The scheduled hearing is being dubbed as a victory for Patel as his lawyer alleged that Australian authorities had failed to supply requested documents in his extradition case.

The hearing could lead to a fresh bail bid by Patel, who has been held in a US prison for over two months on charges of manslaughter, and also delay his extradition hearing set for June 26 in Portland by three weeks, an AAP report said on Monday.

Patel, who hails from Jamnagar in Gujarat, was denied bail by the district court in April.

Last week, Patel's lawyer, Marc Blackman, had claimed that Queensland police Sergeant Graham Walker advised him on May nine that documents in the extradition case would be sent to the US.

However, Blackman said the documents did not arrive and there was "no explanation for the delay".

The lawyer told US District Court judge Dennis Hubel that the delay constituted special circumstances warranting 58-year-old Patel's release from prison on bail "pending the extradition hearing".

Monday's hearing was held via a teleconference, with Patel, 58, likely listening in from jail.

The surgeon, dubbed as 'Dr Death' by the media in Australia, has been at the high-security Multnomah County Detention Centre in Portland, Oregon, since his arrest by the FBI on March 11 on a request by the Australian government.

Australia is seeking extradition of Patel to face 16 charges, including three of manslaughter. He faces three life sentences if convicted on those charges.

Heading: Sir Vidia called ‘mongoose’ in poetic attack - Indian Express
Content:
Syria will allow UN inspectors to probe allegations that the country was building a nuclear reactor at a remote site destroyed in an Israeli airstrike, the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Monday.

IAEA head Mohamed ElBaradei did not say whether his inspectors would be granted access to the site during the planned June 22-24 visit. But a senior diplomat familiar with the details of the planned visit said agency personnel had been told they could visit the facility. The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

The building was flatted by Israel in September. Neither the United States nor Israel gave the IAEA information about the site until late April, about a year after they obtained what they considered to be decisive intelligence: dozens of photographs from a handheld camera that showed both the interior and exterior of the compound in Syria's eastern desert.

Since that time, Syria had not reacted to repeated agency requests for a visit to check out the allegations, using the interval to erect another structure over the site — a move that heightened suspicions of a possible cover-up.

ElBaradei repeated his criticism of Israel and the United States in announcing the Syrian visit, taking Washington to task for waiting so long to brief him on its suspicions, and Jerusalem for its air strike.

"It is deeply regrettable that information concerning this installation was not provided to the agency in a timely manner and that force was resorted to unilaterally before the agency was given an opportunity to establish the facts," ElBaradei said. His comments to the closed meeting were made available to reporters.

ElBaradei noted that Syria "has an obligation to report the planning and construction of any nuclear facility to the agency."

Heading: Love thy neighbour and other lessons - Indian Express
Content:
For years Nobel prize-winning poet Derek Walcott has traded insults with Sir VS Naipaul. Now, he has upped the ante by slamming his old sparring partner in a poem that mocked the Indian-origin author as a "mongoose".

The St Lucian writer composed the poem "The Mongoose" and read it at the Calabash Literary Festival in Jamaica. But, before reading it to an audience, he said that he was going to be "nasty", The Daily Telegraph reported.

Walcott read out the opening lines of the poetry: "I have been bitten. I must avoid infection. Or else I'll be as dead as Naipaul's fiction."

In fact, he has expressed his anger at what he sees as Naipaul's rejection of his Caribbean heritage in order to gain acceptance from the British literary establishment. In particular, Walcott is outraged that Naipaul, whose ancestors were Indian labourers who moved to Trinidad in the 19th century, thanked only Britain and India in his Nobel acceptance speech, but not the country of his birth.

The poem's title refers to an animal that was imported from India under the British empire. As Walcott puts it: "The mongoose takes its orders from the Raj." The poem also attacks Naipaul's later novels Half a Life and Magic Seeds with the words: "The plots are forced, the prose sedate and silly. The anti-hero is a prick named Willie."

Walcott expresses disbelief that this Naipaul can be the same author who wrote A House for Mr Biswas, which won the Nobel prize.

In the poem there is a coded reference to Naipaul's essay on Walcott, published in 2007, which praised Walcott. Both writers have refused to comment on the poem.

However, Patrick French, Naipaul's biographer, said: "Knowing Naipaul, he will say nothing and then at some point he will lash out. He said to me once: 'I settle all my accounts.'"

Heading: A dilemma called oil - Indian Express
Content:
It's finally over and we can now go back to our normal lives between 8 pm and 11:30 pm (What were we doing at that time in our normal lives when there was no IPL? I have no recollection. It'll be a journey of discovery. An archaeological expedition. The term 'lost world' comes to mind. Conan Doyle or Steven Spielberg, take your choice, and pray you don't get eaten).

The first year of the Indian Premier League is over. It has been won by the team on which the least money was spent, and the only one captained by a non-Indian and also a non- 'icon' as defined in the IPL tender documents. The stars of the tournament have been two Australians, Shaun Marsh and Shane Watson, who are not in their national teams, and a Pakistani bowler, Sohail Tanvir, who doesn't even know which is his best foot forward (or, rather, the batsmen facing him have no clue about that).

A tubby Australian who retired from international cricket some time ago has turned out to be the best general in this prolonged war without bullets (and no balls above shoulder height), and two other retired cricketers, Shaun Pollock and Glen McGrath, have shown the world why they will be remembered as great bowlers in every history of the game ever written. All greatness, when analysed, is about simplicity. In this case, it was just accuracy: that old duet of line and length.

And a man called Lalit Modi caught 41 flights in 44 days, clocking up more frequent flier miles than anyone since the Wright brothers decided to test out an idea they had, and guffawed all the way to the bank. Thoughts that trouble me: how much luggage did he carry? How did he manage his laundry stuff? Because he was wearing a different suit every day. Did he buy clothes every time he landed in a city? Did he rent them? Can you rent suits? Did he ever become confused about which city he was in, like, land in Kolkata and tell his driver to take him to the Wankhede Stadium (I have a friend who took four flights on four consecutive days and started making STDs to his own phone)? Does he know where he is right now, or is he filing a missing person report about himself in a city he flew out of last Wednesday?

I'll take a deep breath now and get back to clichés. And — two more deep ones. Ok, IPL will end up (yes, I know, every grey eminence of cricket writing has said this already, but sometimes one has no option but to agree with them) redefining cricket in every form of the game, and our engagement with it. We will demand that our batsmen hit more sixes in the 50:50 version of the game, and our batsmen, when they go out to play a test match, will look at the bowling differently. Bowlers will be more circumspect and less lavish with their ideas. Fielding will be elevated to equal status with batting and bowling. Everything about the game will be tighter.

Yet, the biggest reasons why we love the game will be preserved and accentuated. I speak for myself, and this is what I love about cricket: that there is no better sight in the world than a genuinely fast bowler hitting a batsman on the head (there now, I've revealed my secret dark side), or a spinner fooling a batsman totally and seeing him go back to the pavilion shaking his head in puzzlement (the softer, though perhaps more sadistic, side). It was proved in 20:20 too. Shoaib Akhtar ripped through the Delhi line-up with sheer pace; he was just faster than anything his victims had seen or imagined. And the pure guile of a Warne or a Muralitharan will always remain a delight and a wonder.

The next year of the tournament will be fascinating. Or rather, the commercial decisions that will fashion the next one. Players will be up for sale, and the franchisees will have to make a trade-off between success on the field and money in the bank. Shane Watson was bought for three years for $125,000, a pittance compared to what Rahul Dravid was paid. Whoever owns the Rajasthan team will have to take a call, trade him for a million dollars, or keep him in the team with an eye on retaining the trophy. Do you keep V.V.S. Laxman or trade him off at a loss for Shaun Marsh? And what does a Hyderabad team mean without Laxman leading it? IPL should be a management case study and perhaps a management book. The issues to be probed here are many more and much more complex than those one considers when launching a detergent or rebranding a consumer durable. Cricket in India is about life itself. Add to that the moneys involved, and the challenge is Everest-stakes and exhilarating.

And lastly, what we also learnt from IPL is that we love the cities we live in. Or the ones that we think we belong to. Through the tournament, we cheered for players we thought were ours, even if they came from a small town in Chhattisgarh. And it worked the other way too: Manpreet Singh Gony experienced Chennai, and Chennai gave him all the love it could garner. Above all, just the sight of a Gony playing for Chennai, a Sri Lankan opening the innings with Tendulkar, a Pakistani being the spearhead for Jaipur, Ricky Ponting playing for Ganguly and Kolkata, this is what the core values of sports are about. The IPL enabled us to embrace our foes, forget our differences, and at the same time, paradoxically, celebrate our identities and love our neighbours, and we are all neighbours in this flat world. It has been a great trip.

Sandipan Deb, former editor of 'The Financial Express', heads the RPG Group's forthcoming magazine venture sandipandeb@yahoo.co.uk

Heading: Fashion’s Pied Piper - Indian Express
Content:
The government does little or nothing to stem the losses being racked up by the public sector oil marketing companies and sooner than later these companies start rationing petrol and diesel. The consequent consumer backlash, particularly from the farmers whose sowing season will have been disrupted, heralds the beginning of the end of this administration. Or, the government does indeed raise prices, rejigs tax rates and whatever else required to pull the oil companies back from the brink of financial collapse. But then in the aftermath, the Left parties withdraw support; the government loses its majority in Parliament and the Congress party is pushed into elections under unpropitious circumstances.

The Webster dictionary defines 'dilemma' as a difficult situation; a predicament that compels a choice between two unattractive options; the space between a hard rock and a stone. The government is today wedged tightly in this space. It is struggling to extricate itself but whatever it does now will seem to be too little too late.

How have they got themselves into such a spot? India is not, after all, the only country that is reeling under the twin burdens of historically high oil prices and unprecedented volatility. China, Pakistan, Malaysia and Indonesia have all adopted policies to shield their consumers from the brunt of high prices. They have implemented them without distorting the structure of energy demand or undermining the viability of their domestic industry. Why is it that in India we have not been able to secure a similar balance?

One could, of course, place the blame squarely on the nature of our politics. We have been in an election mode ever since oil prices started their upward march. This has limited the manoeuvrability of the Central government to align domestic prices to international trends. Also, the Left has hardly been cooperative. However, this is in my view too generic a response. It suggests that our political system is fundamentally regressive.

I have a more specific explanation. It has to do with inter ministerial turf battles, lack of leadership and the weakening hold of the Central government over state governments. Let me explain this point through the structure of the price buildup for petrol and diesel.

Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) calculates inter alia the landed import duty paid price of petrol and diesel every fortnight. This calculation is based on a formula that is linked to international prices. IOC's landed price of petrol in Mumbai for the second fortnight of May was, for instance, Rs 38.1 per litre and for diesel Rs 48.8 per litre. The marketing companies had to, in other words, pay this amount to the refiners to buy the products. Next, the Central government imposes an excise and educational cess on the purchase cost. In May, this was Rs 14.4 per litre and Rs 0.4 per litre for petrol and Rs 4.6 per litre and Rs 0.1 per litre for diesel respectively. The total cash required by the marketing companies to purchase petrol and diesel in May was, therefore, Rs 52.9 per litre for petrol and Rs 53.6 per litre for diesel. The companies then sell these products at the ministry of petroleum mandated price of Rs 49.7 per litre for petrol and Rs 35.6 per litre for diesel (Mumbai prices). As such, they lose Rs 3.2 and Rs 18 for every litre of petrol and diesel sold respectively.

That, however, is not their total loss. They have to also pay sales tax to the state governments. In Mumbai, this tax is Rs 10.6 per litre and Rs 7.1 per litre for petrol and diesel respectively. Thus, the total cash loss suffered on account of the sale of 1 litre in Mumbai is Rs 13.7 and Rs 25.1 for petrol and diesel respectively. This is, in other words, the amount by which prices would have to be increased at the retail outlet for the companies to simply break even on a cash basis. Such a hike is, of course, out of the question.

The logical solution should be a package that combines a price hike with a reduction in the central and state tax rates. After all, central and state taxes account for 32 per cent (diesel) and 50 per cent (petrol) of the price build up. But logic gets tossed aside in the face of turf and power battles. The finance ministry will not forego its windfall gain; the top leadership will not force a compromise between the petroleum ministry and the finance ministry. And the Central government does not have the clout to compel the state governments to countenance a reduction in their revenues.

The consequence of this stalemate is now coming home to roost. The oil companies are, of course, close to bankruptcy. But more egregiously, we are now seeing a distortion in energy consumption patterns. The domestic price of diesel is today less than the price of furnace oil (internationally among the cheapest of products that come out of a refinery). This is encouraging a switch from furnace oil to diesel and in consequence a sharp hike in the consumption of diesel. Its demand growth is now exceeding 20 per cent per annum. The 'dieselisation' of the economy is also making a mockery of efforts to secure energy independence.

Everyone will have to bear the implications of adhocism in policy. This must not, however, take away from the urgency of mitigating the longer-term consequences. Even amid the twists and turns of current policy my hope is that the government will look to placing petroleum policy within the bounds of a more sensible economic and pricing framework. What should be the drivers of such a framework?

First, we should accept that high oil prices are here to stay. This does not mean we will not see sharp declines from present levels. What it does mean is that we will not see prices stabilising at levels significantly below a triple digit number. Second, we must create a mechanism that leads to a 'graduated' reduction in subsidies, an orderly alignment of domestic prices to international levels and a more efficient disbursement of financial support to the poor. Third, we must reverse 'dieselisation'. And finally, we must recognise that the sine qua non of energy security is a robust and competitive domestic petroleum and energy sector.

The writer is chairman of the Shell Group of companies in India. Views are personal express@expressindia.com

Heading: Distasteful, in brief - Indian Express
Content:
A couple of decades ago, long before India had a Fashion Design Council or a fashion week, French designer Yves Saint Laurent had made his presence felt in a minuscule circle of Indian jetsetters with his heady fragrance, Opium. Typically, YSL, the perfume, was strong and made a statement about YSL's alleged addiction to narcotics. The legendary couturier died of a tumour in Paris at age 71.

Old timers in the Indian fashion industry will remember YSL's spectacular show in Delhi opposite the Purana Qila, and in Mumbai at the Gateway of India in 1989. YSL's business partner, Pierre Berge, came down to Delhi with 20 French models and a huge team of make-up artists, costume designers and clothes assistants. The brief to the choreographer of the show from the iconic Laurent was to celebrate India's history and majestic monuments.

Laurent's gowns, each one a delicately embroidered showstopper, were the perfect contrast to the Old Fort and the choreographer for the event, Harmeet Bajaj, remembers it as one of her grandest shows, ever. "The whole scale of the event was simply huge," says Bajaj. "No expense was spared on props, special effects or even flower décor." YSL held private showings at The Oberoi the same year for a handful of wealthy Indian clients. For his show in Mumbai, a French model in a catsuit descended from the top of the Gateway, suspended on a rope. India had never seen anything like it before.

YSL's contemporaries include the wildly popular designers, Karl Lagerfeld and Balenciaga, whose design legacies will probably outshine YSL's in time. However, it's unlikely that working women in cities all over the world could forget his most significant contribution to feminine clothing: making the black pant, a must-have item in every wardrobe. YSL's masculine touch in women's wear came about at the ideal moment, when women had more power to spend.

Delhi-based designer David Abraham of the label, Abraham & Thakore, has vivid memories of a retrospective of YSL's works at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. "YSL was big when we were in NIFT. He changed contemporary fashion completely and his work will remain influential," says Abraham. YSL's fashion empire extends to South Korea and Japan. In India, his shades are a big hit. Tikka Shatrujit Singh, representative for Louis Vuitton in India, recalls meeting him in Paris some years ago. "He was very courteous and he loved India. He told me he found the colours here very inspiring," says Singh.

He was at his peak till the '90s after which YSL sold a part of his company, whose profits had begun to dip alarmingly. A pity, since the luxury segment market in India has just taken off.

leher.kala@expressindia.com

Heading: Degrees of dumbness - Indian Express
Content:
Let's talk about a subject that is not the normal topic of conversation here. This is not about elections, film stars, cricket or crime. You've seen that, heard that, that and that. There's nothing more to be said about them except that we look forward to seeing elections (because we travel more around the countryside than with Travel & Living), less of film stars (Shah Rukh Khan, are you reading this? Amitabh, Abhishek and Aishwarya, will you please take your next padyatra to Siddhivinaayak temple at 3 am, incognito?) — and no more crime and its punishment or cricket. Sometimes, too much of a good or bad thing (cricket and crime, respectively) is enough.

So let's leave the Rajasthan Royals to enjoy themselves at everyone's expense, leave the Aarushi Talwar-Banjade murder mystery to the CBI, and concentrate on a brief history of underwear. Specifically, men's underwear. Particularly, men's underpants. First of all, let's ask a question to SRK's super brats on Panchvi Pass: why would anyone name underwear Midas Premium Briefs? Because he wants them to turn into gold? But why would any man in his right, wrong or any sense wish to adorn himself in gold underpants, unless... what ?

Perhaps we should abandon this unprofitable path of sociological discourse. Why is it that every TV commercial for gentlemen's undergarments makes you so not want to buy the thing, thong, whatever? Why is it that every TV commercial for male underpants (and we're being very generous calling that thing-thong, underpants) always ends up staring at the suitably attired part of the male anatomy — and then hastily looking away?

Last week, we happened to sight Frenchie in the middle of a saas and her bahu. It's suddenly changed: the first time we saw it, the camera allowed a lady and a gentleman to look at one another with bedroom eyes before leapfrogging towards the Frenchie that happened to be so much in love with the man, it clung to him as perhaps Romeo did to Juliet — or was it the other way around? Then, someone somewhere realised that this TV commercial was invading a very private affair between the man and the Frenchie. So now when we encounter The Man and Frenchie it is from a considerable distance — with the camera averting its gaze just before contact with Frenchie.

The obvious associations between underwear and sex are too obvious to be restated. The only point to make is that if we are going sexual, let's not be coy about. Or else find another more tasteful way of selling underpants.

When it is not Sex, it's Spartacus or some such movie. Here, the undergarment becomes a potent weapon that transforms the man into Charlton Heston. Don't believe us? Well, when was the last time you saw the Dollar Club Big Boss TV commercial? Here, a muscular man, in crimson red briefs that cling to him with greater adhesive power than Araldite, Quick Fix, prances about, carving up the harmless looking air with a menacing sword with muscles bulging from the bursting suitcase of his chest — playing Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon on a rooftop with a lady in tattoos? What does it all mean other than the creator of this dreadful commercial has mixed up his movies — like we have?

Earlier TV commercials such as Lux Cozy or Amul followed the same idea of women being irresistibly drawn to male underwear — with or without the man. Those, if you recall, were withdrawn after protests to the I&B minister.

These TV commercials have nothing to recommend them. They should be taken off (the commercials not the briefs) or sent to the cleaners.

shailaja.bajpai@expressindia.com

Heading: SBI kicks off farm loan waiver scheme - Indian Express
Content:
Really, don't we all know by now that finding examples of teens' and twentysomethings' ignorance is like shooting fish in a barrel? If you want to exercise your eye-rolling or hand-wringing muscles, take your pick. Two thirds of high-school seniors in America, 2006 couldn't explain an old photo of a sign over a theatre door reading COLOURED ENTRANCE. In 2001, 52 per cent identified Germany, Japan or Italy, not the Soviet Union, as America's World War II ally. Mark Bauerlein sees in such ignorance an intellectual, economic and civic disaster in the making. In his provocative new book The Dumbest Generation: How the Digital Age Stupefies Young Americans and Jeopardises Our Future (Or, Don't Trust Anyone Under 30), the Emory University professor of English offers the usual indicators, grand and slight.

The old have been wringing their hands about the young's cultural wastelands and ignorance of history at least since admirers of Sophocles and Aeschylus bemoaned the popularity of Aristophanes ("The Frogs," for Zeussakes?!) as leading to the end of (Greek) civilisation as they knew it.

Historical memory is essential to a free people. If you don't know which rights are protected in the First Amendment, how can you think critically about rights in the US? Fair enough, but we suspect that if young people don't know the Bill of Rights or the import of old COLOURED ENTRANCE signs — and they absolutely should — it reflects not stupidity but a failure of the school system and of society (which is run by grown-ups) to require them to know it.

A more fundamental problem is what Bauerlein has in mind by 'dumbest.' If it means "holding the least knowledge," then he has a case. Gen Y cares less about knowing information than knowing where to find information. IQ scores in every country that measures them, including the US, have been rising since the 1930s. Since the tests measure not knowledge but pure thinking capacity — what cognitive scientists call fluid intelligence, in that it can be applied to problems in any domain — then Gen Y's ignorance of facts (or of facts that older people think are important) reflects not dumbness but choice.

Bauerlein is not the first scholar to pin the blame for a younger generation's intellectual shortcomings on new technology (television, anyone?), in this case indicting 'the digital age.' But there is no empirical evidence that being immersed in instant messaging, texting, iPods, videogames and all things online impairs thinking ability. Even videogames might have cognitive benefits, beyond the hand-eye coordination and spatial skills some foster. No one knows what kids will do with the cognitive skills they hone rescuing the princess.

Heading: Patel seeks tax cuts on jet fuel - Indian Express
Content:
The State Bank of India (SBI) on Monday kicked off the UPA government's mega farm loan waiver scheme -- the Agriculture Debt Relief & Debt Waiver Scheme 2008. The bank's Jamli rural branch in Madhya Pradesh issued fresh loan eligibility letters to farmers under the scheme.

SBI chairman OP Bhatt visited the Jamli branch to assess first hand the level of preparedness. "SBI's nationwide rural branch network is geared to implement the scheme. Under the Scheme, agriculture loanees need not apply for debt waiver, the bank will do it for them," Bhatt said.

Bhatt distributed fresh loan eligibility letters to 21 farmers who are eligible for debt relief under the scheme. In SBI's Bhopal circle, consisting of MP and Chhatisgarh, an estimated 1.80 lakh and 67,000 farmers in the two states respectively, eligible for benefits under the scheme by way of waiver or relief.

Bhatt directed the bank staff to implement the scheme within the set deadline and also extend fresh loans for the ensuing Kharif season as per requirement of the farmers.

Only those direct agricultural loans which fulfill all the three conditions — disbursed between March 31, 1997 and March 31, 2007, overdue on December 31, 2007 and remaining unpaid until February 29, 2008 will be eligible for debt waiver/debt relief under the scheme.

Loans for construction of storage facilities are not covered under the scheme. Loans for purchase of land, construction of farmhouses, sheds, fencing, etc. are also not covered under the scheme. Only direct agricultural loans to farmers are covered under the scheme.

Heading: More airlines hike surcharge - Indian Express
Content:
Expressing "extreme unhappiness" over the steep 18.5 per cent rise in aviation turbine fuel (ATF) price, civil aviation minister Praful Patel today said that he discuss measures to mitigate its impact with Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and Finance Minister P Chidambaram next week.

"We are taking a serious note of the matter. The increase in jet fuel prices will hurt the sector in a big way," Patel told reporters. "Some airlines have informally told me they are thinking of either pruning or rationalising their services," he added. Jet fuel prices ex-Delhi have jumped 62 per cent to Rs 58,388 per kilo litre in May this year from Rs 36,149 per kl last April.

Fuel currently forms around 45 per cent of an airline's operating costs and this will go up with the recent price hike. Internationally, the price of fuel has gone up at least 5-6 times between 2004 and 2008. Fares on an average have, however, dropped during the same period, Patel said.

The minister also stressed that Indian oil companies have been charging a much higher price for jet fuel compared with international benchmarks. On an average, ATF in India is priced 65 per cent higher than other countries.

For instance, Indian carriers bought ATF at Rs 55,191 per kl in April 2008 (ex-Mumbai) while jet fuel cost just Rs 32,387 per kl in Singapore. Estimates by the Federation of Indian Airlines (FIA) indicate that a cut in ATF price by 60 per cent has an impact of lowering airline operational losses by 25 per cent. A drop of even Rs 1,000 per kl translates to an annual savings of Rs 500 crore for the sector.

Patel said the Centre had long been lobbying with states and the finance minister to reduce the sales tax, customs and excise duties on jet fuel. "Even a uniform 12 per cent sales tax on ATF is not going to help now. Only a declared goods status on ATF (with a 4 per cent sales tax) will help."

While most states have kept the sales tax high on revenue considerations, experience suggests that volumes rose manifold when the tax is cut. Andhra Pradesh, which reduced the sales tax on ATF from 30.55 per cent to 4 per cent between 2002 and 2004, saw a 60 per cent increase in ATF uplift by erstwhile Indian Airlines. Similarly, when the Chattisgarh government cut it to 4 per cent from 25 per cent, it resulted in an increase in jet fuel uplift by 200 per cent by Indian Airlines.

Ministry estimates also suggest that sales tax on ATF constitutes only about 1.5-2 per cent of total state sales tax revenue. "The high growth in consumption of ATF coupled with an increase in basic cost of ATF will ensure that even if states cut the sales tax by 50 per cent, the impact on revenue will be minimal," the ministry had said in a note to the empowered committee of state finance ministers.

Heading: Tata Motors hikes prices - Indian Express
Content: Taking a cue from state-owned Air India, airlines including market-leader Jet Airways, Kingfisher and Deccan have also decided to hike their ticket prices, starting tomorrow. Jet Airways has increased the fuel surcharge on short haul flights (up to 750 km) by Rs 300 a ticket while long haul flights (beyond 750 km) will cost Rs 550 more per person. The UB group owned Deccan-Kingfisher combine has also announced a similar increase in prices, starting tomorrow.  With this increase, passengers would be charged Rs 2,250 as fuel surcharge on short haul  routes and Rs 2,900 as surcharge on long haul flights. The fuel surcharge in May last year stood at just Rs 900 per ticket, indicating a three-fold rise in the fuel burden passed on to consumers.

Heading: House panel flays steel policy - Indian Express
Content:
With input costs rising across the board, Tata Motors has raised the prices of its compact cars by 1-2 per cent and that of its utility vehicles by 2-3 per cent.

"Tata Motors today announced an increase in the prices of its passenger vehicles. The increase is effective from today. The increase on the Indica, the Indigo and the Indigo Marina is in the range of 1 to 2 per cent. The increase on the Sumo and the Safari is in the range of 2 to 3 per cent. The price increase was necessitated due to the continuous increase in input costs," Tata Motors said in a statement.

Tata Motors' decision to increase the prices of its products followed that of Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai's hikes during the last month.

Heading: Videocon to acquire international telecos - Indian Express
Content:
Describing the National Steel Policy as not a structured one, a Parliamentary panel has said it is grossly inadequate in addressing the burning issues in the steel sector like grant or renewal of mining leases and securing environmental clearances, which could impede its growth.

"The Committee feel that NSP is not a well structured policy. NSP does not propose any concrete mechanism to address important issues such as problems faced in grant or renewal of mining leases and inordinate delay in obtaining environmental clearances etc which hamper the growth and development of steel industry," the Parliamentary Committee on Public Undertakings said in its report.

It argued that all corporate plans and expansion plans of steel PSUs such as SAIL and RINL, which are being implemented in pursuance of the goals of NSP will be adversely affected if the difficulties are not addressed in the right earnest.

"The Committee are disappointed to find that NSP is too inadequate in addressing the burning issues." As regards the delays in obtaining clearances, the Committee said though NSP proposes a single window clearance for large projects to be followed by statutory clearances by the ministries concerned, it does not clearly spell out a time frame within which clearances should be granted. Observing that mineral-rich states would recommend renewal of existing leases only against credible mining investment plans against a specified period, the Parliamentary panel said NSP has failed to spell out clear-cut modalities in this connection.

"The Committee are unsure whether the mineral-rich states would follow the guidelines of the Central government in a federal democratic set-up," it said and suggested that the NSP should emphasise on creating a single-window mechanism for all the clearances and timely and adequate availability of steel and discouraging export of quality iron ore needed by domestic steel utilities. Steel production capacity in the country by the year 2012 will be nearly 124 million tonnes. India is expected to become the second largest steel-making nation in the world by 2015.

Meanwhile, the country's crude steel production has grown at more than 10% annually from 34.71 MT in 2002-03 to 53.90 MT in the last fiscal while the production of finished steel stood at 55.27 MT during 2007-08 as against 40.71 MT in 2003-04. Sponge iron grew at a CAGR of 22% to reach a level of 18.35 MT in 2006-07 compared to 7.68 MT in 2002-03.

In tune with the NSP, state-run steel giants SAIL and RINL are in the midst of ambitious expansions to adopt the best technology and double their production capacities. SAIL's Rs 54,000-crore expansion plan is expected to raise its capacity to 26.2 million tonnes per annum of crude steel production by 2010 while RINL's expansion plan is expected to take its capacity to 6.3 million tonnes and is expected to be completed by February 2010 at an estimated cost of around Rs 9,000 crore.

However, the Committee expressed concern over SAIL's lower blast furnace productivity as compared to Tata Steel and RINL, ostensibly due to inferior iron ore content and higher impurities, and asked the PSU to bring it on a par with the others.

•India expected to become 2nd world's largest steel-making nation by the year 2015

•The country's crude steel production has grown at more than 10% annually from the 2002-03 figure of 34.71 MT to the last fiscal's figure of 59.30 MT

Heading: ‘Subsidies can’t go on’ - Indian Express
Content:
The Videocon group is looking at acquiring telecom operators in high growth markets through Thompson, an electronic and picture tube manufacturer. Vidoecon has 30% global share in the picture tube market through Thomson.

"We feel this is the right opportunity to expand and take places in international markets along with India," said Ravi Sharma, CEO of Datacom. "Thomson is present in international markets. Therefore, we are talking to international telcos through Datacom," said Sharma. He said that the company was also looking at Greenfield projects.

The company has ambitious plans for domestic market. It will soon invite expression of interest from telecom vendors for supplying equipment and setting up a network 70 million GSM lines. The company has licence to set up nation-wide telecom network.

As and when the company invites bids for 70 million GSM lines, it will be the second largest procurement of GSM lines from a single operator. The government-owned Bharta Sanchar Nigam Ltd's (BSNL) tender for procuring equipment and setting up network of 90 million GSM lines is the largest tender.

Datacom plans to invest close to Rs 12,000 crore during next four years. The company has already got GSM spectrum for five circles. These circles are Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Orissa. Department of Telecommunications (DoT) is expected to give it licence for rest of the circles by the end of this year. The company has ambitious plans to acquire 50 million customers in less than five years.

The company was also in talks with foreign operators for equity partnership. "Yes we are ion talks with many foreign players for a possible tie up and equity partnership," said Sharma.

The company has appointed Morgan Stanley as its banker. Videocon group chairman Venugopal Dhoot recently said that some Middle East based telecom operators have shown interest in it.

Heading: Sensex plunges on politics - Indian Express
Content:
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh today gave his government's first clear stance on fuel price hike stating that India cannot insulate the consumer fully from the impact of global commodity prices and oil price inflation.

Referring to the government's policies of not raising prices of scarce natural resources such as water and oil, Singh pointed out that kerosene prices were left untouched in the last four years. "Even petrol prices did not fully reflect world trends. In the case of water, we have been altogether imprudent. This situation cannot continue forever," he said, addressing the annual general meeting of industry chamber Assocham.

Though Singh said in as many words that rising petrol and diesel prices was inevitable, his United Progressive Alliance government is still trying to build a political consensus on the imperative for such a hike. The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs is slated to meet Wednesday to discuss options including rising LPG prices by Rs 20 a cylinder and that of petrol and diesel by Rs 2 and Re 1 a litre, respectively.

The Prime Minister said while the government was focused on reversing the recent surge in headline inflation that touched 8.1 per cent for the week ended March 19, it was keen not to hurt the "rhythm of the growth process''. "I do not wish to see a return to the era of blind controls," he said, referring to demands from a section in the government to invoke provisions of the Essential Commodities Act that go against the grain of market reforms.

At the same time, the Prime Minister drove home the importance of fiscal prudence. "To ensure the stability and sustainability of the growth process, we have to follow more prudent fiscal policies. We cannot allow the subsidy bill to rise any further," he said, adding wider political consensus was need to adopt more rational economic policies.

According to Singh, the unrelenting rise in crude oil prices and a growing threat of protectionism from developed countries can spell disruptive consequences for countries such as India. "It (rising crude oil prices) can have adverse consequences for the global war against poverty. We need a new global compact between oil producers and the developing world. We need global leadership."

Lambasting the developed world for following protectionist policies when developing countries are standing their ground in the face of increased challenges of globalisation, he said, "It is regrettable that the forces of protectionism are gaining political ground in many developed countries….I hope that the developed countries will not forget the development dimension of Multilateral Trade Negotiations. It takes two hands to clap."

Developed nations crying foul and seeking protectionism, was not a happy role reversal, he noted, comparing the situation to a decade ago when developing nations were seeking similar benefits.

"There is no reversal of roles possible until we are able to create a more equal world," he said, adding India had a strong stake in the successful outcome of the Doha Round of Trade Negotiations.

The Prime Minister blamed the rising global commodity prices, in particular food prices, as the reason for developing countries to impose controls on commodity exports and increase subsidies on imports.

Heading: Former Sebi top honcho lands plum post at ING - Indian Express
Content:
Bears tightened their grip on the market as concerns on the inflation front, weak cues from the European markets and possible political uncertainty at the Centre pulled down all major indices after the bourses opened on a positive note. The Sensex, which hovered around the 16,200 level for some time, plunged by 352.39 points, or 2.15%, to close the day at 16,063.18 points. The Nifty plunged by 130.50 points, or 2.68%, to close the day at 4,739.60 points.

Said PK Agarwal, President, Research, Bonanza Portfolio Limited, "markets tried to continue the Friday's up move initially. Nifty went to crucial resistance zone of 4908. It remained positive for the first two hours. But after Prime Minister's statements regarding concerns on fuel prices came and one of the UPA supporters (RSP) moved away from the co-ordination committee, a sharp selloff was seen. After European markets opened weak, the selloff accelerated."

Banking and real estate stocks were the worst hit amidst fears of further monetary tightening by the RBI. Unitech, TCS, Nalco, SBI and ICICI Bank were among major losers. However, some buying interest was seen in Hero Honda, Sun Pharma, Maruti Suzuki and Dr Reddy's.

Some experts also attribute Monday's fall to the political confusion caused by the Left Front constituent Revolutionary Socialist Party which decided to withdraw from the UPA-Left Coordination Panel.

Heading: Hyundai, Skoda buck sluggish trend - Indian Express
Content:
Former Securities and Exchange Board of India chairman M Damodaran has been appointed as the chief representative and advisor for ING in India. In this non-executive role, Damodaran will work with the management and partners of both ING's banking, insurance and investment business units.

"Damodaran's distinguished career, as well as his wide network of relationships in the Indian financial sector, makes him a valuable addition to ING. His recognised expertise will significantly contribute to the execution of our growth strategy in India," said member of the executive board for ING group, Eli Leenaars.

Damodaran's predecessor in Sebi, GN Bajpai, is also in the financial services sector now. Bajpai, who was the chairman of LIC before becoming Sebi chairman, is now the chairman of Future Generali India Life Insurance Company.

Damodaran has a work experience of over 30 years in financial services and public sector enterprises.

In the past, he held various roles with the ministries of finance, commerce and information & broadcasting. He has also worked with the Reserve Bank of India. In July 2001, he was appointed chairman of Unit Trust of India, country's largest mutual fund promoted by the government.

Damodaran also served on various committees set up by the Centre as well as the RBI to reform the banking sector. He was also elected chairman of the 80 members emerging markets committee of IOSCO.

HIGH FLIER

•Damodaran has a work experience of over 30 years in financial services and public sector enterprises.
